House resumed consideration in Committee of Bill No. 21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire-Mr. Borden. (Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)
On section 2:

Mr. Chairman, I am sure it is gratifying to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to find that hon. gentlemen on the other side are able to open their mouths and to say something in connection with this great question which has been before the House and the people for several months past. It is gratifying to us because we feel that if the gag has been loosened to hon. gentlemen on that side of the House it certainly will be loosened to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. I listened with a great deal of pleasure to the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) before the House rose at six o'clock. I felt sorry for that hon. gentleman at one time during his speech because, when he undertook to tell a joke, he was unfortunately the only one who laughed at it. He found a great deal of fault with this side of the House for its lack of enthusiasm. I am sure that if there has been a graveyard without any new burials during the last three months it has been found on the other side of the House. Very seldom has any hon. gentleman opposite opened his mouth on this question to defend the policy that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Borden) brought in before the House in December Mr. LANCASTER.
of last year. I am sure that if any enthusiasm has been shown at all, it certainly has been shown on this side of the House. On a memorable Saturday night some little time ago there was enthusiasm enough on this side of the House to suit hon. gentlemen opposite and if there is a repetition of it to-night they will probably get all the enthusiasm they desire.
The hon. gentleman went on further to say that he really believed that there were some hon. gentlemen on this side of the House who did not believe in any contribution at all. I would like to say to the hon. gentleman from Brantford that ,if he could see into the innermost depths of the minds of some hon. members sitting behind him, he would perhaps find some who were not in favour of a contribution and not in favour of doing anything for the Mother Country. We are prepared to do something, to do just as much as hon. gentlemen opposite although perhaps we may not talk so much about it. We are prepared to show our patriotism and to do something for the Mother Country.
I was amused to hear my hon. friend from Brantford refer also to the visit of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to Toronto the other night. It seems to have stirred some hon. gentlemen opposite, and some of the Conservative newspapers, to think that the right hon. gentleman could go to Toronto and, after filling the largest place in Canada, hold a meeting from which thousands were turned away. It shows that the Liberals in the good old province of Ontario are not all dead and that when they have an opportunity to do so they will speak with no uncertain sound. Even the members of the Tory party in Toronto were so eager to get to this great Liberal meeting that not knowing there would be any room for them, they had to forge tickets enough to enable them to attend. I hope the lessons that they received there will do them good and that they will be able to change their policy in a great many respects.
Then, the hon. member for Brantford found fault with my hon. friend from St. John city (Mr. Pugsley). I have no brief to defend my hon. friend from St. John. Hon. gentlemen opposite have found out during this session that that hon. gentleman is fully capable of taking care of himself. If the hon. member for St. John was looking after the interests of that port I want to ask why the hon. member for Brantford should find fault with hiin. is strange that the hon. member for Brantford, a manufacturer in the province of Ontario, as I am informed, does not seem to have any great love for the Maritime provinces. He, and others like him, exhibited that feeling at the election on September 21, 1911, when they turned down the reciprocity agreement which would have given the Maritime provinces larger

and better markets and put them on the road to prosperity, a road which they will not get on for many years to come. In the eloquent peroration with which the hon. gentleman closed his speech, and he is certainly a good speaker, he appealed to this side of the House and said: Let us bury the hatchet. The Liberal party buried the hatchet, and the axe also, in 1909, when the House voted unanimously for a Canadian navy in reference to the defence of the Empire. I do not think it comes with very good grace from an hon. gentleman opposite to talk of burying the hatchet at this time. He went on to say that he hoped we would stand up to-night and vote with the Government. He will find that we will stand up and vote, but I do not think there will be many members on this side of the House who will vote for the proposition brought down by the right hon. leader of the Government. I have, I imagine, about fifty reasons why this Bill should not pass, and at this stage of this discussion, with the gag tightening around our throats, I do not propose to occupy much time.
I am opposed to it because it is a measure brought into this House for the purpose of extricating the Tory party from an unpleasant position in which they found themselves when they so unexpectedly were placed in the Government seats, which do not fit them, and which they will not occupy after the next election. Then again, I am opposed to it because the people, or some of them only, were deceived by the cry that an emergency existed, and that Great Britain and Germany were on the verge of war. But we have not heard the word ' emergency ' used by any hon. gentlemen opposite for some months. Even the Prime Minister's voice is restored to its natural tone, and not trembling with emotion as it was when he read his pastoral address in introducing the resolution last December. I am convinced more than ever that no emergency then existed, and that it will not be found to exist in the distant future when Germany and Great Britain will have a further agreement as to the building of warships. I further conscientiously believe that the present proposal of the Government has not made the relations between these two great nations any more cordial.
I am opposed to it again because it is neither a gift nor a sane business proposition. At one time we are told by the Government it is a gift, and then again they say there are strings to it. I presume the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier), the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Nantel), and you, Mr. Chairman, will each have a string, and then, if the Nationalists of Quebec still object to Canada doing anything for the Motherland, they will pull these strings and deter the dreadnoughts from being the most powerful dreadnoughts that ' science can conceive and money buy ' ever do any effective work either in the North sea or tied to the rock of Gibraltar, with all the members of a mongrel government having strings to them and pulling against each other.
I am opposed again to the voting because I firmly believe, feeling as I do our obligations as one of a galaxy of nations within the Empire, that we owe something to ourselves and to those we are bound to, by the strongest ties of a free and autonomous people, and therefore we should at once without delay commence the building of ships and carry out the Laurier naval policy of establishing a navy of our own, with the proper dignity and self-respect of this our young and optimistic nation, thus manifesting that we are true to our heritage and destiny. During the last election the Tory headquarters at Yarmouth had across the whole front of the building the motto:
' Canada for the Canadians.' At the next election I would suggest this motto for their headquarters:	' Canadian workingmen's
money for British ship-builders, and armour plate monopolists.'
I am opposed to the Bill again because I do not believe it commands the respect and endorsation of a large majority of the people of Canada, and after the discussions and difference of opinion that have been expressed I do not know that the people of the Motherland will accept the proposal of the Government at all, and I think they would not be doing justice to a large part of the people of Canada if they did.
We emphatically believe on this side of the House in the building of our own ships, the inauguration of ship-building plants; in short a Canadian built, owned and manned Canadian navy controlled by the people of Canada through its representatives in Parliament, ready at all times to defend and protect our own coasts as well as our ever growing and expanding trade routes. We believe that by pursuing such a policy we shall in a truly patriotic way be rendering aid to the Empire and doing justice to ourselves.
Liberalism stands to-day as it has always stood for enlarged freedom and a strong and deep patriotism. It does not proclaim its loyalty from house tops and on public platforms at election times, but is ready at all times to render aid to the Motherland, not in a grudging manner, or by the application of the gag or closure, whichever you may call it, which throttles free speech, the greatest and most inestimable gift ever enjoyed by a free and independent people, and which shatters the greatest safety valve we had before its application, and which puts back the hands

on the dial of our national clock at least a hundred years.
Again, I am opposed to the Bill because it does not provide for these three ships to be built by tender and contract, by which public competition can be taken advantage of and no doubt thousands of dollars saved to the people of Canada. Why, I ask, is this principle not adopted in the expenditure of this tremendously large sum of money, when it is well known that all expenditures of $5,000 or more in the construction of public works must be done by tender and contract.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to this Bill because it is money to be spent outside of Canada and has never had the approval of the people of Canada. Therefore, I submit, Sir, the electors whose, money it is, should have an opportunity to express their approval or disapproval before one dollar is spent. In view of the widely divergent views and open opposition to this measure, I maintain that the people of Canada should be appealed to.

privilege to represent a number of coloured people in this Parliament, and if the hon. member (Mr. Gauvreau) made that remark as an insinuation against the coloured people, I want to repudiate and resent it on their behalf. Mr. Chairman, as a young member of this House, I desire to congratulate the Government on having the courage and the legislative capacity to enact rules that have made it possible to carry on the business of this country. I feel, as I rise to address this House tonight, somewhat as Paul felt when he was released from prison and permitted to return to his own church, because I now have the right to express my view. That right was heretofore denied to me because about a dozen members of the Opposition monopolized the whole time of the House. Talk about closure! Talk about gag! If anybody in this House has been gagged, the supporters of the Government have been gagged, owing to a few of the leading members of the Opposition monopolizing the time of the House. Three hour speeches! Members opposite making bets in the corridors that they can speak eight hours and then talking about the right of free speech.

We are pleased to hear the hon. gentleman again and to see him at liberty. It is always unpleasant to the well-regulated mind to see another in prison or in durance.
I desire to refer to the lemarks of the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) in his speech yesterday. Speaking of the measure before the House he said:
This is a measure which the people of Canada have been demanding for six years. The majority of the people of Canada, I believe, have been willing to contribute to assist in maintaining the supremacy of the Empire and to share in the expense which is incurred thereby.	I
I do not believe that the people of Canada demand or desire the measure that is before the House. I believe the hon. gentleman is right in his second statement, that the majority of the people of Canada have been willing to contribute to a system of maintaining the supremacy of the Empire and to share in the expense thereby incurred. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are just as willing as any hon. gentleman opposite to support this view, and it is utterly unfair for hon. gentlemen to say that this is not the case. It is true that we have different ways of doing things; we believe that a certain course which we advocate would be in the best interests of the country and tend to the security of the Empire. My hon. friend also referred to the statement I
Mr. WILCOX.
of the right hon. leader of the Opposition that when England is at war, we are at war, and that it does not follow that because we are at war we are actually in the conflict. The hon. member for Red Deer asked a very pertinent question in connection with that, and the answer of the hon. member for Vancouver was surprising. Speaking about the Afghan war, he said that it was not a war, but only an expedition, yet in that conflict an entire regiment of Highlanders was practically destroyed. Who is to decide whether or not a conflict is a war? If we are to be guided by the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver in regard to this matter, we are going to have another emergency-that of deciding who is to determine whether or not there is war. Apparently the conflict in which the killing of a whole regiment takes place in not a war. I fancy my hon. friend is not a Highlander or he would have more sympathy for those unfortunate persons who were killed in Afghanistan. However, he had a little more to say in regard to that matter:
I should say that undoubtedly Canada should take part in any war that might occur there. I say further that I care not where conflict might be, if Great Britain was at war with any country on the face of the earth and, if it were necessary for Canada to participate in it, undoubtedly she should do so.
He says: 'If it is necessary for Canada to participate in it,' and the hon. gentleman therefore himself admits that there may be wars in which we should not engage, and that the right hon. the leader of the Opposition is right. The hon. gentleman is to be complimented for that, although I do not say he has dealt as fairly with it as he should have done, he has been fairer than any other hon. gentleman on the other side of the House. My hon. friend seems to agree with the first proposition laid down by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition, that when England is at war we are at war, and all parts of the Empire are at war. I am not going to quarrel with that proposition, because we all admit that. The next argument is the one to which our friends opposite are apparently opposed, but the hon. member for Vancouver practically said that was right, because he said that only in case of necessity should we be engaged in the conflict. Who is to decide whether or not that necessity exists? We claim that the Government should decide whether or not that is necessary. If it is true to-day that when the Empire is at war we are at war, it was also true in the eighties. Within a few years three very serious wars were engaged in by Great Britain, in Zululand, Egypt and the Soudan respectively. Following out this principle, we were at war when England was at war, but we were not in the conflict. Facts are stubborn things, and hon. gentlemen oppo-

site cannot face the facts and justify the political, capital they ma*ke out of the statements of the right hon. leader of the Opposition by saying that which they cannot back up and which they know is entirely unreasonable. The hon. member for Vancouver makes a rather remarkable statement in that connection. Referring to the statement of the right hon. the leader of the Opposition that when England is at war, we are at war, and that it does not follow that because we are at war we are actually in the conflict, he says:
How any person could entertain such contradictory views as these is beyond nay comprehension.
But he himself entertains those views; he positively stated them before he was through. Some hon. gentlemen have given their views as to the dividing line between the parties with regard to this great question. I shall not quarrel with any of those views, but I wish to repeat what I said when first addressing the House in regard to this matter, that the real dividing line between the parties is the dividing line between a policy of centralization, followed by the members of the Government, and their supporters, and a policy of self development supported by hon. gentlemen on this side of the House.
I listened with great attention to the remarks of the hon. gentleman from Welland (Mr. German) last evening, and, though he expressed his views in this regard in different language, they were practically the same as mine. The desire shown by the Government to retain in their own hands to the exclusion of Parliament the expenditure of money is caused by their desire to centralize, and our desire to oppose them is because we want to develop our own country and our own institutions. Their original desire to have the ships built in England and placed in the North sea was caused by their faith in the policy of centralization, and they are the legitimate successors of the members of the Family Compact of old days who desired centralization by Downing Street rule. It is true that there is in our country a spirit of Canadianism which makes it impossible for hon. gentlemen to go so far as members of the Family Compact went, and therefore they have not done so.
My hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) told us last evening that his forefathers took part in the struggle for selfgovernment in Canada. I am in the same position as my hon. friend. If my hon. friend and I, as well as other hon. members on this side of the House, were to take any other ground than that we are taking now in the same great struggle, we would be unworthy descendants of our forefathers who fought for self-government in Canada. One thing that makes me a
little proud of my pedigree is the fact that my father and grandfather were engaged in that struggle during the whole of their lives and I am going to continue in it.
The joint resolution of 1909 has been the subject of considerable discussion in this debate, and we have heard the rather surprising claim made on behalf of the Government supporters that the present Bill is in accordance with, and in furtherance of, the principles laid down in that resolution. In every Bill that is brought before this House, there is some great central dominating principle, some dominating object round which the other provisions centre, and I think it will be agreed that the central and dominating object of the resolution of 1909 was the speedy construction of a Canadian naval service for the defence of Canada and of the Empire. I think that is unquestionable. That was the central thought, the central idea, in the minds of the hon. members of this House so far as I could gather from the resolution itself and from the debates in connection with it. It is true there was_ a secondary object, as there generally is, and that was to express our readiness to make a contribution to the Empire in case of immediate need or emergency. I do not care which term you use. The two dominating ideas of that resolution were first, the speedy construction of a Canadian naval service for home and Empire defence, and secondly, a contribution in case of an emergency. I do not think that the right hon. the leader of the Government will deny that these were the ideas, and yet the right hon. gentleman tells us, perhaps not in the exact words that I am using, that the Bill before the House is carrying out the principles and objects of that resolution. Strangely enough, he tells us that this is not a contribution at all. Surely it is not carrying out the other object; and if it is carrying out neither the speedy construction of a Canadian naval service, nor the idea of a contribution, what is it? According to my right hon. friend's own words, it is not in any sense, carrying out the objects of that resolution of 1909. It is entirely contradictory to it, because the carrying out of the terms of the Bill would be the greatest factor in the speedy construction of a Canadian navy.
We have heard a great deal about an emergency, but as my time is limited I think I will have to leave it out. It has pretty well escaped, and I do not think we can do anything more now than chase it. Anyway we need not worry ourselves about it.
It gets out of the way.

It is gliding; it glides
as gracefully as my hon. friend from North Essex (Mr. Wilcox) did from imprison-

ment to liberty. If there be an emergency, the proper way to meet it is by a money contribution. That would be the most natural way of meeting it. I fail to see how the present proposition would meet an emergency, assuming there was one. My hon. friend from Vancouver, (Mr. Stevens) made a suggestion in connection with this. He said he is not quite satisfied, that he himself believes the contribution would be best, a contribution of ships. I say that if we give a contribution in the case of an emergency it would be better to give a contribution of money. The reason for that is clear. If we ourselves were in any particular need or danger, which we could not see ahead, it would be pretty hard to know in advance exactly what we would want, and if the British Empire were in danger from any outside source, the best way to meet that danger would be to give a cash contribution which the British Government could use in any way they saw fit. However, as my time is nearly up, I do not wish to follow that matter any further.
With regard to assistance in the case of an emergency or need, we on this side of the House are prepared to do everything required to assist the British Empire in naval matters. The only difference between us is as to how this should be done. We must remember that the British Empire includes Canada, and that Canada requires defence as well as any other part of the Empire, and if we are able to do anything for the defence of the Empire generally, we might at least start at home. If we built our own vessels and placed them on our own coasts, they would be of as much use in defending the Empire as if they were placed anywhere else. If required anywhere else, it would be an easy matter to send them. We are told that vessels from the British navy can be sent from the centre to the circumference, and surely it would be as easy to send them from the circumference to the centre.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman's time has expired.

For the past two months we have not heard the supporters of the Government on this great question, but I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister upon allowing some hon. members on the other side to express their views to-day on this great issue. I am sure we have gathered some interesting information from their speeches, and I am only sorry that they are not being allowed to continue to give us their views. Hon. members on the other side must have received orders that they could no longer speak this evening. There is a thinking bureau in England Mr. THOMSON (Qu'Appelle).
composed of able men, and these gentlemen give their time and study to the best naval defence possible of the British coast. We have also in this country a thinking bureau composed of the members of this House and of the Canadian electors. For four years we have all been thinking very seriously about the best way of defending our coasts and protecting the British Empire. We were at one time of one mind in the matter of the defence of our coasts on the Atlantic and the Pacific. When we were of one mind, we were, from the point of view of our friends the Conservatives, good and loyal British subjects. The hon. member from Frontenac has the same opinion of himself now as he had then in reference to the naval defence of this country. But he is on the other side of Mr. Speaker now, and he cannot speak in this House without first attacking our honoured chief in the most un-British and unfair manner. If the hon. member was wrong in 1909 and 1910, what about his dear and loyal subjects now? How many hours of sleep has he lost since last December? Have we had the benefit of a fair discussion of this great question on the part of the supporters of the present Administration? In their minds they may have dropped the Laurier naval policy, but they have been disciplined by a few of the ministers to keep silent upon the question. They were ordered not to take part in the discussion of this great issue and if any one of them dared to speak, he was reprimanded in much the same way as was John's wife upon one occasion when she and her husband paid a week-end visit at an English castle. There was a wealthy business man who received an invitation for himself and his wife to spend a weekend with a well-known aristocrat. At breakfast, on the morning following their arrival at the ancestral castle, Mrs. Noveau Riche, in trying to chip off the top of an egg with her knife, exercised so much strength that the egg was knocked out of the cup and rolled under the table. Not knowing the correct thing to do in such [DOT]circumstances, she appealed to her husband. 'John,' she whispered, 'I ^have dropped an egg. What am I to do?' 'Do not cackle,' replied the matter-of-fact John. Our hon. friends opposite have almost dropped the naval policy and when they appealed to their right hon. leader he said to them: 'Do not cackle.'
The Pacific coast at this moment needs a few vessels and we have lately had a lesson from our friends in New Zealand and Australia with regard to this phase of naval defence. With the permission of the committee I shall read a brief article published in the Vancouver Daily News, upon

the question of Pacific coast defence. This is what it says:
The question vitally affects this province. We have vast interests on our coast demanding protection. The Premier of the province, the Navy League and papers of both political parties have frequently drawn attention to our defenceless condition. We are endeavouring to enforce an immigration policy which is devised to keep this a white country. Must we expect aid from the Australian fleet or the British China squadron? How much better it would be if all the dominions on the Pacific joined with the British China fleet in forming a formidable force to protect the coasts of the British dominions washed by these waters! But there is an economic aspect of the question which also concerns this province. We require permanent industries; new centres of industrial activity. These would be created as a corollary of the organization of a Canadian naval force. We would see the development of an extensive sliip-building industry in our waters which would give us a pre-eminent status among the maritime nations who will soon be fighting for the trade supremacy of this great ocean. The Prime Minister of Australia recently uttered a striking expression in discussing the defence problem. ' What would be our answer to a threat of war ? * he asked. ' It would be the clang of five thousand hammers on the anvils of our country/ So should it be with Canada. The people should be given an opportunity to decide this question and it should be decided at once.
I was amused at the remarks of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) who spoke before six o'clock. What a great man he is in his own mind when he speaks of the British Empire! Let this Parliament give the people of Great Britain a preference of fifty per cent instead of thirty-three and a third, and what will ibe the state of the Imperialistic mind of my hon. friend? It would be like his steak under the potato. In his essays on naval defence, Vice Admiral T. H. Colcomb, alter making some allusion to the invasion scares- which every now and then startled the British people says:
We may look upon the Empire as an immense commercial speculation. The base of operations is English money, which is laid out in investments in all parts of the world. Upon the freedom of communication the commercial existence of the Empire depends. From this point of view, the greatest calamity which can befall this gigantic enterprise is that pressure from without which would threaten to cut off the greatest number of its communications. That danger may, any day, assume a very visible form in the shape of a powerful foreign fleet in the channel. The capital of the greatest commercial enterprise in the world could not be more effectually locked up than by the suspension of ' imports/ and exports; *which would, as a consequence, follow such a contingency.
For the reasons we have briefly given, it is evident that the safety of the channel must be maintained; and that it is worse than
useless to distribute the forces for the protection of our commerce over various parts of the world, while the base of our naval operations, the most vital spot in our commercial system, remains insecure. As this involves the employment of a large sea-going fleet for channel service only, it is advisable to ask the question. Will not a fleet sufficient for this purpose be equal to the task of protecting England from invasion?
There is a thinking body in this country who will soon speak, I hope, upon this great issue. There is a body of advisers who hold the destiny of this Dominion in their hands and it is the electors of Canada. The members of this great thinking body, Sir, are, first the manufacturers. What will they say about the spending of this $35,000,000 outside of Canada? Will they have tiheir share of this money? If, not, what will they say as electors of Canada at the next election? What will the farmers say, who compose the great majority of the people of this Dominion? They want a share of this money in the sale of their products to the labour class. Then, what about the labour class? The labour man is entitled to a part of this money. He has to pay a high duty on everything that he buys to support the administration of this country. If the Government wants to be generous to this particular class of the Canadian people let it give a preference on -the British goods which are brought into Canada. They would buy their hats, clothing and their underwear much cheaper in many instances than they can procure these articles in this country. England needs our cheap farm products to-day more than a gift of $35,000,000. Great Britain needs the help of our young men on board of Canadian men of war. The British Empire wants a test of our loyalty, not in money, but in our presence in the firing line in case of need.

I want to deal with this question from another point of view than that from which it has been considered so far. I want to deal with it from the point of view of the autonomy of Canada as well as to present to the committee a few considerations showing the dangers attendant upon Imperial federation. If we read history as far back as 1790 and compare the manner in which colonies were treated at that period with the way in which they are treated at the present time we cannot but shiver at the expression 'Imperial Federation,' as a dangerous step towards the prevention of the development of our country.
One might say, and rightly so that conditions have changed since; that many in Great Britain have become educated of the importance of our Dominion that our natural resources have been the subject of consideration by the capitalists of the

Motherland; that a large amount has been and is now being invested in our country; that the manner in which colonies were treated then cannot be feared at present. All these things may be true, but we must bear in mind, that if our great and vast country has prospered, it is no fault of the great Imperialists. For, outside of furnishing money at a respectable interest, they have done nothing to stimulate, to encourage, to change conditions of a century ago or more, and the policy of let well enough alone might be applied to them in this present case.
The masses to-day are reading, are studying, are comparing conditions in all their forms, and as great producers of wealth they are afraid of embarking in a policy of Imperial federation. Now, Mr. Chairman, let us see some of the effects of such conditions of a century past. We read in ancient history that the great men of Downing Street thought rightly or wrongly that colonials were nothing but serfs; a negligible quantity, and only good enough to wring from them whatever productive power they then possessed. The occupants of the large House that formed the end of that cul-de-sac so well known then as it is to-day by the name of Downing Street, thought then as they do now, that they could control the whole Empire. Colonists or others at that period could talk of the Crown, of the Parliament, or the public; they could talk of the honour of the first, the wisdom of the second, the knowledge, the opinion, or the rights of the third, but, Mr. Chairman, at that period neither Queen, nor Lords, nor Parliament, and less, the public itself, could exercise any power, or could vindicate their rights, or their will. We must bear in mind. Sir, that the destinies of the colonies, then, were in the hands of Downing Street. One can say that there must have been appeal to the Crown, and so there was, and this privilege was more than once exercised by the public, but without any success, for the reason, that never did such an appeal, go further than that office. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, I ask the hon. member from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), if such incidents were to repeat themselves, would we be justified, in having anything to do with such a body of men.
If we go deeper into the probable effects of such a federation, it is more alarming, for again history and common sense teach us, that the same powers may at any time use their knowledge, and their activity, to force their views, on any one human being who may be sent to represent Canada. What have we to gain by leaning towards this idea? Must we bind ourselves to the views of one or two or half a dozen men? In a democratic country like ours, the Mr. VERVILLE
mentality of our citizens will not now, and I hope never will accept, to be governed by others than themselves.
We have seen our country grow in a marvellous way in recent years; we have developed in a sphere other than that occupied by the occupants of Downing Street, and I really believe that our prosperity is-the subject of jealousy, from these so-called benefactors of society. I claim, Sir, that we have no right to take any steps which may lead us to such a federation. The people of the country do not want it, and this present policy would, I have no doubt, drag us into this federation. Leaving aside the expressions of members on. the other side-of the House, and looking at the question in a cool spirit, in a common sense way, no-one can conclude differently. My firm belief is that those hon. members who now sit in this House, and have Imperialistic ideas, do not represent the majority of their constituents. I am convinced that the majority of members to your right, Sir, do/not: represent any such ideas. I will ask them now whether it is not better to have confidence in our own citizens, who know the country, who know its needs and the laws required by these needs, than to be governed by an Under Secretary of State in the-British Isles, who does not know even the country he is supposed to submit legislation for.
Our vast country has risen from her slumber of years ago. She has taken her place amongst nations; she has turned her face to the briliant sun of prosperity and activity, and no one has the right to enact, any law, that would have for its effect the diminishing of our national pride. It is not very long ago, Sir, that a great Lord had to mourn over our destinies, or rather mourn over the future of the Dominion, and the oldest settlers to-day can remember that, not any later than 1839 (seventy-four years ago), not a lengthy period in the life of a country, Canada could in no way, be compared, with the republic to the south. Anyone travelling then, had to travel on the only railway then existing which extended for fifteen miles, from the St. Lawrence to Lake Champlain, Montreal then the biggest commercial centre of Canada, could not. be compared with Buffalo, which was almost a new creation. But, outside of commercial centres, the contrast was still greater. What could be found then, in the lower provinces, in Quebec, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick with that 1,000 miles of line of separation? A widely scattered population, pour, and apparently unenterprising, but very industrious. We were then separated by a tract of forest, without towns, and almost without villages, and without means of communication with each other; the people living in small houses, and deriving a mere subsistence, and I may say condemned to eternal misery. But, Sir, what has changed these conditions? Was

it the command of Downing Street or selfdevelopment? The country was to some [DOT]extent in a dormant state until Confederation, hut, the new generation of that time saw that their future prosperity as well as that of the country, rested on the development of their knowledge, their energy, their commercial spirit; and instead of relying on the knowledge of a few enterprising institutions, they picked up their courage, they faced all obstacles in their path, as do the gold seekers in our great mountains of the West, and they set to work to raise themselves to the standard of their cousins on the other side of the line. Now, what has been the success of their endeavours? The generation of 1867, have been the admiration of all the civilized world. They have created enormous wealth; they have developed our natural resources; they have supplied our means of transportation; they have erected our great industries, and set them in operation. They have produced and are now producing for the markets of the world. They have erected large cities and towns in which you will see the finest buildings of the world. They have developed their brain power to such an extent, that, to-day Canada, as a country, stands second to none in proportion to her population. The working masses have borne the largest share in this marvellous development and they have commanded the respect due them, by other class of society. They have through their spirit of citizenship been recognized and rightly so, as bulwarks of democracy which no one can deny. They have on all occasions shown their spirit of gjoderation; they have shed their blood and given their lives to command the respect of our nation.
I ask you now, Mr. Chairman, I ask the members of this House, I ask the country, why our artisans are to be now looked upon as unable to bring to perfection what after all _ is nothing but an industry. Is it not plain, Sir, to anyone, who gives any thought to this great problem, that we are stepping in a wrong direction. Is it surprising to anyone in this House, or out of it, that the masses do not want any legislation passed by this Government that would have for its effect, forcing our country into the clutches of the magnates of Downing Street. Can the masses of this country be blamed if they are jealous of their rights, jealous of the prosperity of what they have created. and if they believe, and rightly so, that any federation other than that which we are now developing would be dangerous for our country, would be un-Canadian, unBritish, and would have for effect the betterment of a few to the detriment of the masses.
Mr. Chairman, if we take the history of the development of Australia and read it carefully we shall be astonished at the
means employed to build up a new country. In this House, from time to time we cite, as an example, the conditions existing in that part of the Empire. Certain classes of society are astonished at the progress of Australia from an economical standpoint. Has this progress been brought about by titled men, by the autocracy of Downing Street, or by the democratic spirit of the inhabitants of Australia ? No one would ever have dreamt that a mass of people in a free country could have done so much for the Empire. The masses in that country have prevented to a large extent the introduction of class distinction, and thus have remained free and loyal subjects of the Empire. . We expect to do likewise in our great Dominion, and for this reason let us keep away from Imperial federation.
Mr. Chairman, I have stated in this House that, if we kept on enacting dangerous legislation, we would incite the masses to some kind of a revolution. On all occasions my remarks have fallen on deaf ears. I suppose that our hon. friends opposite have made up their minds that a warning of this nature, coming from the most feeble member of the House, should be brushed aside, and that, instead of preaching a doctrine of this kind, I should preach one of peace and harmony amongst the great producers of wealth of the country. The man is not yet born who can preach such a doctrine with any good result under present economic conditions. Every time that a ray of sunshine appears on present conditions, it seems that the power of money and the power of industries, wherever they are, cover them with a cloud of self-protection, of centralization of power, to crush the legitimate demands of the majority of the people of any country, and we will say then, as representatives of the people, that we are empowered to legislate even against our autonomy. All these things, Mr. Chairman, are of a nature to create amongst the masses a stronger feeling of discontent than existed before.
if the Parliament of Great Britain, as far back as 1689 and 1776, lost its prestige, and if a blow was struck at the authority of hereditary monarchy, a veritable revolution in the political life of England, it was because of the oppression which the masses resented, and because the rank and file said that iron rules could not be tolerated any longer. I will admit that present conditions cannot be compared with those of a century ago; but nevertheless an imposition of the character of the one that we are about to pass at present, .if giving away our revenues perhaps to ouy a few titles, or to step into the federation of dreadnoughts, is for our present generation as bad as conditions were in the seventeenth century for the masses in England.

Mr. Chairman, I call on the present Government not to proceed any further with this dangerous legislation. I call on the ministers of the Crown not to force on me and on those that I have the honour to represent, legislation that may _ have the effect of creating an enormous disturbance in our economic world. I call on the Government not to interfere with our present rights-our present autonomy. The people of this country expect to receive, from those whom they have sent to represent them in Parliament, more than a submission to the gTeat power of Downing street.
I call on the Minister of Labour (Mr. Crothers) to intervene, on this present occasion especially, in order to protect and to safeguard the interests of those whom he is supposed to represent. If my hon. friend does not believe my assertions; let him ask the labour men of the country by petition or otherwise, what their sentiments are on this very important matter, and he will then see that the policy which he is now supporting so energetically is not supported by the majority of our population.
I may be told, Mr. Chairman, that I am mixing economics too much with politics. It is a question whether you can make or discuss politics without introducing the question of economics. If the members of this House were to study the legislation brought before them from its practical point of view, they could not refrain from stepping into the economic field, because the great political questions of the day are becoming more and more economic questions. In order to corroborate my assertion, we only have to look around continental Europe as well as at our friends to the south, and to judge from present occurrences, to see how the economic question comes more and more to the forefront of politics. One may judge also, from expressions made on the floor of this House, intentionally or otherwise, that every one has to some extent spoken in favour of autonomy. If economic questions have taken their place in politics, it is because of the natural feeling of jealousy of the poor towards the rich, and of the debtor towards the creditor. It finds its interpretation in the fact that our country has prospered so tremendously. The development of her commerce has excited the jealously of the civilized world. Our industries are the pride of our nation, and all these things have come about because of our autonomy. These are very good reasons why we should fear Imperial federation. Mr. Chairman, why should we be interfered with? Have we not enough trouble of our own? Even at home with all our riches, our minds are constantly occupied with our own operations. Our difficulties have proceeded largely from economic as well as from national and political causes, and such expenditure in a strange Mr. VERVILLE.
land will surely lead us to severely tax our industrial resources. Commercial and industrial considerations must weigh more with us, if we are to secure our position in the Empire.
Mr. Chairman, these questions are_ not by any means the only considerations. Let those of us, and it should be allfwho>
wish to help and to maintain the advancement and progress of our country, must seek to answer clearly the economic questions that are pressing themselves upon us, by looking at them in the right light- the one afforded to us by the history of a great industrial Dominion. That great question can also he applied to our great farm producers. They have already acknowledged its effect. They know full well, that any departure from our present system of autonomy would effect the downfall of their prosperity.	,
Over sixty per cent of our population cannot be looked upon as possessing an inferior knowledge of the needs and the future of our country. It is through sacrifices that they have risen to their present condition. It is through their spirit of citizenship that they are now commanding the markets of some parts of the world; and, true to their principles, they also ask not to be governed from Downing street. Must we blame them? Must we blame the great industries for being suspicious of the doings of a handful of men who are trying to force legislation that will have the effect of creating a few more millionaires? From that standpoint it is more dangerous, and I am surprised that the present Government still insist on returning to ancient history, because servitude and slavery have for all time to come been abolished. Modern legislation, democratic action on the part of government, is what the people want and expect to receive.
