Go on.

Nowhere can we see
an example more striking of Imperial federation and its effect in benefitting a few than in England herself prior to or about the time of the industrial revolution. The business men of Great Britain then, as now, wanted to regulate the trade in the colonies, and nowhere do we see more clearly, the combination of national policy with class interests. The intention of legislation then was to require that the colonies should be entirely subordinate to the Mother Country, and that their trade and industries should be regulated, so as to.

increase at once the political power and the wealth of the class in control of the Mother Country's a Hairs. Legislators at that period had only on? object, that is, what seemed hest for their national policy, and they were strongly supported by merchants and manufacturers whose private interests it was to keep the colonial trade as far as possible in their own hands.
What were the colonies, after all, at that period? They were looked upon as markets for the Motherland, from which you could draw as you saw fit and which you could command as you saw fit, if you happened to be a member of the controlling element of society.
What was the objeet then of the great merchants in establishing the West Indian colonies? It was merely a device to support a few moneyed men to the detriment of the colonials themselves.
What can be the objoc-t of our Imperialists who are now sitting in this House? What can be the object of those travelling through the country to preach this gospel of Imperial federation? What does it all mean? It means that they are not even satisfied with the enormous profits made by them on the operations of trusts and mergers; they wish this Government to go beyond its legislative power. They wish this Government to favour a mode of operation that would have for effect the making of an adjunct to the Motherland of our great Dominion. The present Government, by acquiescing in the demands of the jingoes of the land, would no doubt, create closer friendship with the money power of our country. They would receive, I am sure, titles, which I am invited to believe some are anticipating. They would form an aristocratic class, as in the Old Country, thus abolishing the spirit of democracy which has dominated in our Dominion. They would, by so doing, produce a strong feeling of distinction of classes in our population. They wouli succeed, I have no doubt, in creating a sentiment of revolution, which it is	the special purpose	of a
democratic government to prevent. They would centralize the productive activity of our commercial industries for the benefit of a few. They would control our imports and exports, also our modes of transportation. They would increase taxes to such an extent that Canada would diminish instead of increasing in population. In summing up, Mr. Chairman, they would be, masters of the country. They would command all, even the Crown. They would establish a system so disgraceful that we should be a country of slavery instead of a free and emancipated people. My remarks may appear severe, but when legislation is brought before Parliament the passing of which may bring about the conditions I have just alluded to, it is my duty as a representative of the people to protest in the strongest possible language permitted by this House, and to bring to light the consequences of an Imperial federation.
Mr. Chairman, you may tell me that the present Bill has nothing in common with such a federation. But it has been said and proven by members of this House, as well as by newspapers supporting the present Administration, that the passing of this measure will inevitably draw us into the mechanism of Imperial federation, and take away from us our autonomy of which we are so proud. Australia, a colony governed by a democratic government administered by a labour party, have lately, as you know, approved in its entirety the policy propounded by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition in this House. I am proud to say, Sir, that the Canadian policy is approved by my fellow-workingmen of that part of the Empire, and time will show, I am sure, that other colonies will also approve the spirit of democracy, the broad-mindedness of the present leader of the Opposition.
Another reason why we should keep our absolute autonomy is the growth of the Canadian people. The number of the citizens who have left the land of their birth, to come to the land of the free is very large, and should be taken into consideration. The mentality of our population, from its cosmopolitan composition, cannot be regarded as likely to be satisfied with laws that would have for effect the withdrawal of our autonomy. Our immigration law and the announcement of our country's prosperity have had for effect the landing on our shores a mass of people from all parts of the world. These people become loyal subjects of His Majesty, they are living in harmony and in conformity with the usages of the land of their adoption, and have become true and law-abiding citizens. Before they left the land of their birth they believed, and they believe now, that they were coming into a colony of the British Empire which had a government of its own, which enacted its own laws governing and administering its own affairs in conformity with the constitution granted to us in 1867. They knew that we were living under British rule and under British institutions; they knew that such institutions are safeguarded to their liberties; they expected that their rights and privileges would be protected to the fullest extent. They knew that Canada, as a colony, had full autonomy. For all these reasons people from all parts of the civilized world responded to the call of our Government to breathe the atmosphere of liberty.
Would it be possible, Sir, after what we have done-could we call ourselves loyal

to our promises, if we should by a scratch of the pen substitute another legislative power over our destinies? What could be expected from our population as at present composed under such conditions? Have we ever stopped to consider what the effect upon our country would be if the different nations we now have, as well as those occupying other colonies of the British Empire, were to become dissatisfied with our mode of government? The great statesmen of our country as well as those of Great Britain have foreseen such an effect. The great leader of the present Opposition has, on more than one occasion, expressed himself in that respect, and always in the same way-in favour of conciliation amongst different nationalities which composes the population of our Dominin.
Mr. Chairman, I claim that those whom are now preaching this doctrine of Imperialism are the worst enemies of the Empire. 1 have no doubt that some are convinced that centralization would be in the best interests of our nation. There may be a few, Mr. Chairman, whose convictions are sincere, but the majority are preaching selfinterest, regardless of the state of things that may be brought about by such a policy.
The population of the Motherland cannot be compared with the population of Canada, as the great majority of the people of the Old Country were born in the British Isles. The development of their mentality has been conducted in another sphere. Tuey have suffered, it is true, but at home, and one can stand more in his own home than in the home of a stranger; not that he does not wish to brush aside the conditions which compel him to suffer, but physically and mentally he can stand more. Can we ask as much from those who come from a strange land? It cannot be expected of them at once; it will take more than a generation to change the customs of foreigners coming to our country-common sense teaches us that you could not expect the contrary. In facing those conditions would we not be justified in proceeding in a cautious way in that respect? Not that I fear, not that I even doubt the 'sincerity or the loyalty of our foreigners to the Crown-far from it, but up to the present time nothing has been done to awaken that spirit of nationalism amongst our great population, and this is the chief reason why we are prospering. If we were to take separately each nationality composing our population, and study their mentality and the effect of each on Imperial federation, I have no doubt that we would find it a very difficult problem to solve. Why should *we create a stronger feeling of discontent amongst our population? Why should we say that the conditions under which our foreign population have lived for years, Mr. VERVILLE.
from the political point of view, are not ideal for our great industries, as well as for our great financial interest. Do we expect that a policy of this nature would be thankfully received by the masses of the country? If we do, we must be absolutely ignorant of our present economic conditions.
Mr. Chairman, I refuse to believe that those who are in favour of sacrificing our autonomy to an Imperial federation are moved by any other motive than the good of our country, but we shiver at the very idea when we stop to consider its effect from every point of view. I, for one, Mr. Chairman, want the Government to be recorded on this very important question, for, As the Opposition is already on record as being against any law that would involve even a shadow of federation, it would seem that the Government should do likewise, so as to keep our population in peace and harmony. Not many years ago the labour men of this country were pressed by many who thought that the labour interests lay in the formation of a Canadian federation. Organized capital did all it could at that time to inculcate in the minds of organized labour that they as organizations had no autonomy. The campaign of discrimination against international bodies found its way even into our chambers-and why? Because it was then believed that the labour organization of our country were governed by a Downing Street-that is, from the United States. I remember the trouble we had at that time to educate our legislators that we had our full autonomy. We were jealous of our rights on the economical field, and we fought by all the legitimate means at our disposal those who were misinformed as to our situation, and that economical fight was to safeguard our full autonomy. Can you understand now, Mr. Chairman, why we are now fighting for autonomy in the political field. The labour men of this country, whether organized or not, will, I am sure, unite in a common cause for liberty, and if necessary a strong appeal will be made in that respect to our brother workmen from the British Isles.
I have expressed the feelings and sentiments of the labour men of my county, and I hope to see the day that the Minister of Labour of the Parliament of Canada will have practical knowledge enough to be in unanimity with those he is supposed to represent. Let us not only protect but grant the full rights of those producers of wealth; let us be loyal to our constitution; let us legislate in conformity with the mandate we have received from our constituents; let us respect whatever feelings the different groups of our population may possess; let us live in peace and harmony with the full possession of our autonomy.

I
was very much impressed last night by the arguments laid down by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German). I think he truly appreciated the spirit of this Bill when he said that the basic principle of the policy of the Government was centralization and control by the British Government and that the policy of the Opposition was that of the preservation of responsible government. He enunciated the principle that Canada should assume her duties in regard to defence, as she had in the past with regard to her national development and the building up of her great public works, and that the Canadian Parliament should control Canada's naval as well as her other expenditures. Why have the Government adopted their present policy? My impression is that the Government was very much embarrassed, and that the Prime Minister was hesitating between two divergent opinions which had taken root in his party. In 1910 he said that Canada should not undertake any policy of naval defence without having a voice in the foreign policy of the British. Empire, and a great number of his party desired that something should be done immediately, without waiting until Canada had such a voice in Great Britain's foreign affairs. The Nationalist party did not want to do anything until Canada should be represented in the Imperial councils. The Prime Minister has decided to make a contribution of $35,000,000, without deciding whether or not Canada shall have a voice in the foreign policy of the British Empire. I am surprised that the Prime Minister, who is a very logical man, should deem it advisable that Canada should make a contribution of $35,000,000 without having a voice in the foreign policy of the Empire. I think the policy of the Government is very illogical. In 1909 the Liberal party, endorsed by the Conservatives, started upon the policy of creating a Canadian navy. In 1910 the Liberal Government put their policy into operation by passing the Canadian Naval Service Act. As my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) said last night, that Act is still on the statute book. The right hon. the Prime Minister made a promise to the Nationalists that he would erase it from the statute-books, it is still there. If the present Government desired to have ships built they did not require to bring in another Bill this session. They could have had the ships built under the Canadian Naval Service Act -of 1910.
Then there is the question of control. In presenting this Bill to the House in December last, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said that it expressed the wish of the Admiralty. I do not doubt his word, but I think the policy of the Admiralty is one of control, and that the dominions should pay. It has been the policy of the Admiralty in the past; they prefer to control; they think they can do so better than the dominions, although at the Imperial conference of 1907 the First Lord of the Admiralty conceded that the dominions should build their own navies. He said:
In the opinion of the Government, while the distribution of the fleet must he determined by strategical requirements of which the Admiralty are to judge, it would be of great assistance if the colonial governments would undertake to provide for local service in the Imperial squadrons, the smaller vessels that are useful for defence against possible raids or for co-operation with a squadron.
I understand that in Australia, it is desired to start some naval service of their own. Perhaps, I might suggest that if the provision of the smaller craft which are necessarily incident to the work of a great fleet of modern battleships could be made locally, it would be a very great help to the general work of the navy. You cannot take small craft, such as torpedo boats and submarines, across the ocean; and for warships to arrive in South Africa, or in Australia, or in New Zealand, or in Canada, and find ready to their hand well trained men in good vessels of this kind, would be an enormous advantage to them. It would be an enormous advantage to find ready to hand, men well trained, ready to take a part in the work of the fleet. There is, I think, the further advantage in these small flotillas, that they will be an admirable means of coast defence; that you will be able by the use of them to avoid pratically all danger from any sudden raid which might be made by a cruising squadron.
The right hon. the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have told us recently that the ships which they want to give to the British Admiralty will be used for colonial defence, that they will be placed in a colonial squadron at Gibralter. If Canada were suddenly attacked, either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific, I do not see how thosp lehips could djefend .our coasts. The First Lord of the Admiralty, the Bight Hon. Mr. Churchill, said they would he twenty-three days distant from Vancouver, twenty-eight days from Australia, and thirty-two days from New Zealand. So that they could not defend our coasts in the event of a sudden raid. Therefore, for some years our coasts would be without local defence. In 1909 the intention of the late Government was to provide our coasts with local defence. Canada was to have a squadron on the Pacific, and on the Atlantic. The policy of the Liberal party this year is to increase the naval forces on both oceans, to make it more effective by the addition of a dreadnought, providing one fleet unit for each, ocean. The Government has not announced its permanent policy. They admit that this contribution of three battle-ships-whether it be a gift or a loan, is quite immaterial -is the first instalment, that it is only a temporary policy to meet an emergency



which no longer exists, because for a few months I have not heard any hon. member on the Government side claim that an emergency still existed. It might have existed in the minds of some of them in 1909, because there was a panic at that time, but since then, I do not think they believe that an emergency exists. They are not even unanimous on the 'Government side with regard to this so-called emergency. They have different names for it. The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) called it a need. The hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup) did not know what to call it. He said it was in the air. Well, what is in the air is not very dangerous. They say it is only a temporary need, and that afterwards Canada will evolve some permanent policy. Why not commence now? Why not use the $35,000,000 to construct two fleet units, one to be placed on each ocean, to serve as local defence, and, in time of need, to assist in the defence of the Empire. The difficulty about the policy of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is that it is not permanent. It has no object. He wanted to obtain from the British Government the concession of representation, and he seems to think that we should not evolve any permanent policy until representation is conceded. As my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) said last night, the question is not one of amount, it is a question of principle, ' the basic principle of Canada abandoning her prerogative of responsible government to control the public expenditure. The right hon. Prime Minister has proposed an amendment to the Bill providing that a detailed statement of the expenditure shall be tabled in the House at the next session. But the time to scrutinize the expenditure is not when the money has been spent. It looks like locking the stable door after the horse has been stolen. We will not be asked every year to vote a certain amount according to an estimate prepared by the Admiralty, _ or by the experts of our own naval service. We are asked now to vote $35,000,000, which will be spent in a year, or two years, or three years, and we will get information only after the money has been spent. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) said this afternoon that under our system of government the Government were responsible for their legislation. The Opposition have done their duty by discussing this Bill as fully as possible, although we cannot discuss it as much as we would like, because at 2 o'clock to-morrow morning we will not be able to continue the debate further. We have performed a duty, we have discussed this Bill for a certain length of time, but the Bill, in the last resort will
Mr. PROULX.
be pronounced upon by the people who will give their verdict upon the action of the Government and that of the Opposition. If my right hon. friend would say that, before this money is spent, the Government will appeal to the people I would not have so much objection to it. But if the Government waits for two or three years to hold the election the money will be spent. What then would be the use of submitting this question to the people, even if the Government is punished by being ousted from power?

Does my hon. friend
think that the Government ought to appeal to the people before they expend any money under' the Highway Bill, or any other similar Bill?

That is a very different
question. Under the Highway Bill the money is to be spent in Canada and for the advantage of the Canadian people. I think there was mention of such legislation in the manifesto published by the right hon. Prime Minister before the last election. The country expected that hon. gentlemen opposite, coming to power and finding an overflowing treasury, the result of the excellent administration of the former Government, would spend money for the benefit of the people. This money which is to be spent on highways will certainly be for the general advantage of the Canadian people. But this is an altogether different proposition because the people expected that whichever party should be in power the policy to be adopted would provide for the construction of a Canadian navy, and that in so far as possible, the money would be spent in Canada. I do not suppose that one per cent of the electorate expected that this Government would offer a contribution of $35,000,000 to the British Government as only a temporary policy and would not immediately adopt a permanent policy. If, as I said, the Government, before spending the money, would submit their policy to the people, I would not have as much objection to the passing of this Bill as I otherwise would, but if they wait until the parliamentary term expires, which will be three years from now, probably the money will all be spent and it will not make much difference then even if the people punish the Government by ousting them from power, because it will be too late to change the policy. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, the great difference between the policy of the Government and the policy of the Opposition is that the Government want to delegate to the British Government the responsibility which should properly belong to itself, whilst on this side of the House,

we want to assume the duty of defending our own coasts and at the same time of assisting in the naval defence of the Empire, and, while doing our duty, keeping control of the expenditure.
Like death.

Yes, like death, but you
can provide against an emergency and you cannot provide against death. Look at the condition of Europe to-day. Does anyone think that Germany is increasing her armament just for fun ? Why has Great Britain found it necessary to increase her ships in the North sea? Is it not plain to any man who wishes to see, that there is an emergency and that that emergency will continue until the nations of Europe stop building ships and increasing their armies. The question for us as a loyal daughter of the Motherland, is, how can we best render effective aid, and render it immediately. Can we render immediate aid in this emergency by starting to build a Canadian navy here in Canada ? Why, every sensible man knows that it would take fifteen or twenty years to build these ships in Canada; but even if it took only ten years, the purpose of our building a navy might have disappeared by that time, and effective aid would be too late before these ships were ready to take their places in the battle line.

I believe, Sir, that the people of Canada are behind the Government in their naval policy. It is admitted by alt of us that we ought to render the Mother Country assistance, and the division only crops up between the parties when the question comes as to what form that assistance should take. This Government proposes that to render aid which is worth anything, that aid should be made effective as quickly as possible, and the Opposition urge delay. Do hon. gentlemen of the Opposition contend that there is no emergency because there is not a war raging ? Why, an emergency might occur at any time; one indiscreet captain of a warship might start a conflagration in Europe, so tense is public feeling, and where would Canada be if we adopted the Liberal policy and waited to construct our ships in Canada. And, while these ships are being built here, and while these dockyards are being constructed to build these ships, what about the defence of the Empire in the meantime ? Surely the better policy is to give the Motherland immediate aid, and the only way of giving that aid immediately is by the policy enunciated in the Bill we are now considering.
' Neither must it be forgotten that the naval policy of the Government now propounded, is only a temporary policy. We say we will vote this money and have the ships built in England, because we will have the ships ready within three years and we will present them to the British nation until such time as Canada needs them. For myself, as a young 'Canadian, I do not believe that the people of Canada would at present favour the expenditure of such a vast sum of money as we are told in the memorandum of the British Admiralty would be required to build a navy in Canada. I believe the people of Canada would condemn any government which proposed to involve the country in the expenditure of $60,000,000 in the first place to build dockyards and then the enormous cost of constructing dreadnoughts in these shipyards, and keeping on building them which the policy of the Opposition means, for, as we know, battleships become obsolete in a few years and once we begin building them we would have to continue. I am surprised that hon. gentlemen in the Liberal ranks,' who represent farming communities, would vote for launching this country into the expense entailed by even the fleet units which their leader has proposed. Until the people of Canada become seized of all the facts and circumstances in connection with the building of a navy, and until they realize its enormous expense, I believe before we adopt the policy suggested by the leader of the Opposition, the people should have an opportunity to digest its real significance. During the two or three years that these Mr. FRIPP.
battleships are being built, the people of Canada will have an opportunity to understand what an extraordinary expensive programme is being laid out for them by the proposal of the Liberal party, and the enormous increase of taxation which it will place on their shoulders. I rather think, speaking for myself, that the people of Canada would even prefer paying an annual sum to England to look after the naval defence of the Empire, than to engage in the construction and maintenance of a Canadian navy in our present state of growth as a nation. -
Hear, hear.

That is my private opinion.
I do not think that at the present time the population of Canada is large enough or rich enough to undertake the almost incalculable expenditure necessary for the building of a Canadian navy.
We have heard a good deal in this House about sending this money over to England and taking it away from the labouring people of this country. Well, Mr. Chairman, that comes with ill gTace from the Liberal party. When, in the history of the country, have they ever been favourable to the labouring interests? Why, Sir, had we adopted their reciprocity policy a year and a half ago it would have taken the bread and butter out of the mouths of the worldng people of Canada. Their policy was to put the industrial workers of this country out of business, and to enrich the citizens of the United States. The working people of Canada well understand that the Conservatives have been their real friends in the past, and they will not be misled by any such specious argument. And, even if these ships were built in Canada, would we not have to bring artisans from England to do the work? Surely every member of this House knows that. What the labouring people of this country want is industries that will stand competition against the world and that will be permanently established here for the benefit of our own citizens. I am satisfied that if we proceed, under the policy of the Government, to begin ship-building in a small way with the assistance of the British Admiralty, and to increase the industry in Canada as time and circumstances will permit, our working people will favour such a policy and will in the end reap the greatest advantage from it.
I notice by the latest census returns, and I want to give this idea for what it is worth and as a reason why I think we should pass this Bill unanimously-I notice by the last census returns that a large number of foreigners have come to Canada and that at the present time 120 different dialects and languages are spoken in the Dominion. Now, Sir, while these foreigners are coming to this young coun-

try, it is in my opinion a noble policy for us to impress upon them that Canada is part of the British Empire, and teach them to realize from the very first that Canada is prepared to bear her share in the defence and maintenance of the British Empire. I believe that, by giving this effective and immediate aid, we can best show these newcomers that we intend that Canada shall support the Empire; and, when we support the naval forces of the Empire we are taking our own share along with the other portions of the Empire.

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend who represents the city of Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) does not often favour the House with his views on the various measures which come before us. During the two sessions that he has had a seat in the House, he has been conspicuous by his absence perhaps more than any other hon. member, unless it be the hon. member for West Toronto (Sir Edmund Osier). My hon. friend from Ottawa appears to be an understudy of the hon. member for West Toronto, because on the only two occasions upon which my hon. friend from Ottawa has seen fit to address the House, he has rather scored and criticised the House because the speeches were too long and the business was not accomplished with sufficient despatch. On this occasion he was inclined to congratulate the House on the good quality of the speeches under the new rules. Perhaps he heard the speeches over the telephone or from the gallery; he certainly did not hear them from his seat in the House. To my mind he made a rather extraordinary statement. He said that when this Bill was brought up he expected that it would be accepted unanimously by this House. Where in the world he got such an idea or expectation it is hard to understand, in the face of what his own political friends along with the Liberal members voted for in 1909. He has not been keeping up with the times. He could not have known of the resolution of 1909 which embodied a policy so far removed from this one. He evidently did not know what his leader had said and done in 1909, or he would not have ventured to make that statement to-night.
In the few minutes at my disposal, let me pass rapidly over some of the chief criticisms which I think can be fairly made to this proposal. I know what I say will have no effect on the Goyemment, but 1 shall get it off my own chest anyway and shall have that much satisfaction. In my humble opinion this whole policy from its inception to the present time has been nothing short of a bungle. I doubt if two ministers of the Crown sitting here to-night really know the meaning cf the Bill that they are asking Parliament to pass. I ask
my hon. friend, who is known as the dominant factor in the Administration, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Rogers), if he will explain what _ this Bill means. I ask him whether it is a gift, a loan, a contribution to the British Admiralty, a loan with a string on it, or the beginning of a permanent naval policy. Let him stand up and answer me if he will. No. He has been only a short time in the Administration, and perhaps he may plead ignorance of what took place in 1909. Beside him is my friend the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid), who has had long experience in the House. Will he tell us whether this is a gift, a loan, a contribution, the beginning of a permanent r.aval policy, or what it is? Beside him another member of the Government without portfolio, my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp). Will he vouchsafe the information which I am asking for? There they sit, four, five, or six of them, and not one of them can ratioually explain this policy or tell us what he thinks it to he. That is the position to-day after we have been thrashing this matter out in this committee day after day and week after week.
Half the Cabinet are unable to tell us what the Bill means. It is a policy which was shaped in the first instance upon wrong information. Where the Government went wrong was when they went to England last year and imagined, from what they heard there, that there was some foundation for the German war scare. I believe that the Right Hon. Winston Churchill put one over them, and he knows it. We are getting nothing out of it; he expects to get something; but he may take it out in expectation; we cannot tell just yet. Judging from what transpired in London last year, by the facts as we know them to-day, I believe it is certain that Mr. Churchill took the Prime Minister and liis colleagues into his confidence and deliberately put one over them. There was no German peril. There was no foundation for any German war scare. I believe I aim absolutely correct when I say that this whole policy was launched on the House with the idea that there was a German peril. That at all events was the excuse given. We remember the opening days of this debate, the opening speech of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister when he read the memorandum of the Admir-altv. German warships, German dreadnoughts, German torpedo boats, on one side, in comparison with those of Great Britain on the other. German naval laws and preambles to German naval laws! That was the reason for the proposal of the Government. Let us follow the other speeches. Take the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of Naval Affairs (Mr. Hazen):	column after column devoted to

this German naval scare and comparing the great German navy with that of Great Britain. Take the speech of my right hon. friend the Postmaster General made about that time: he said the theatre of war was to be in the North sea. Who was going to fight us? Why, within twelve hours steaming of Great Britain was Germany, always Germany. On the 18th of December last, in that magnificent oration delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Foster) before he went away, he told us of the German menace. He said: 'where is the danger? not in Asia, not in the Pacific ocean, but in Europe, in the North sea.' He said: ' I want every dollar of Canada's money spent in that scene of conflict.' That is his language. What was the foundation for the policy of Government? What was their reason for it? It was a German war scare which had no foundation on fact and no reality. Members of the Government and hon. member after hon. member spoke of Germany and German armaments as a menace to Great Britain. They only called a halt when the news came in from some of the German sections of the province of Ontario that this would not do, this nonsensical talk, which was nothing short of a menace to Germany and an insult to the good German citizens of Ontario. The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Weichel), in an admirable speech, drew the attention of the Prime Minister to some of the facts. He let him understand that this insult to the German citizens of Ontario would not do in Waterloo and that he would not stand for it. When my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Meighen) went to South Perth, he did not talk of any German peril; it was European armaments that he discussed; and, when the word came from the Hurons, the Bruces the Perths, and the Haldimands, there was no more German war scare talk, no more German armament talk in this House; no more question of Canada's ships in the North sea to fight against Germany; but, according to the latest accounts, as was well said by the hon. member for Bed Deer, we are going to link up with the Malay states at the Bock of Gibraltar.
I submit to the Prime Minister that his was a bungled policy from the beginning.
I am glad the right hon. gentleman is in his seat, because I want to ask him a question. When he returned to Canada, he was loudly acclaimed by the people of this country. He had been congratulated, pampered, entertained, flattered, in Great Britain. He had, as his Minister of Trade and Commerce said, imbibed the atmosphere of old London, an Imperial atmosphere. When he came back his friends in Montreal entertained him. At that meeting he said that he would introduce into this Parliament a Naval Aid Act, and that Mr. GUTHRIE.
if this Parliament did not pass it, he would appeal to the people. I ask my right hon. friend to-night, will he make good that promise? He smiles, but I want to get an answer. Some of us have fairly hard-fighting constituencies, and we want to get ready. I think I can fairly appeal and ask my right hon. friend for an answer to my question.

Let me touch on one or two facts referred to by the hon. gentleman for South Wellington. He said a wonderful meeting was held in Toronto. Yes, it was a wonderful meeting. The ex-Prime Minister and other hon. gentlemen opposite went to that meeting, and in their pockets they carried the resolutions that were to be passed at that meeting. What were the resolutions? To demand of the Senate of Canada that they should throw out the Naval Bill. I rise to a

Somebody has wisely

I want to call the attention of the committee to the continued happiness that exists on that side of the House as shown this afternoon by the hon. member for St. John and the hon. member for Red Deer. When it is so apparent that happiness does not exist with hon. gentlemen opposite, what a lack of wisdom there must be on the other side of the House. The real lack of wisdom centres in the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, and he knows he has made the mistake of his life in the stand he has taken and is taking on this question. Everyone knows this, and the Montreal Herald, that great Liberal newspaper, has told him he is wrong. The right hon. gentleman laughs; I know full well that when he laughs his agony is greatest. The position of the Prime Minister of Canada has been a consistent one throughout. I will not quote his words uttered before the last election, but they were to this effect:	If power is vested in
me, I will go to the Old Country and ascertain from the Lords of the Admiralty the requirements of the Empire, of Great Britain and of Canada, I will act accordingly, and give effective and speedy aid. These were his words, and every word he has lived up to. This Bill is the product of the statement he made. I am not going to read the statement of the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. In brief it was this: That the British Admiralty would accept the powerful aid that Canada would give as provided in this Bill. These were his words, and they are in the memorandum furnished by the Admiralty. But even if no arrangement had been presented to the people of Canada, if the right hon. the Prime Minister, with the reputation that he has, had returned and had told the people: I sat down and consulted with the Admiralty; they took me into their confidence, and as a result, I ask Canada to pass this Bill, this Bill would have been approved of by the people of Canada, as it will be approved of by every Conservative in this House. More than that, it will be approved of by an hon. member on the other side of the House, the hon. member for Sunbury and Queens (Mr. McLean) who voted for the resolution. We have been told that secret conferences took place between the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues and the Admiralty. Why should there not be secret conferences between men of their high position ? Would hon. gentlemen have England's position blazoned forth to the world? It is only a short time ago that Lord Roberts spoke on the condition of affairs existing in England, and he was blamed .by the British press for having exposed the weakness of England. Let me take
another case. When a prisoner is condemned to death, and an appeal for executive clemency is made, the trial judge's report is laid before the Minister of Justice and his colleagues, but I ask hon. gentlemen opposite whether any one of them would move that that report should be placed upon the table of Parliament and made public to the world. It would not be done, and it never has been done in a capital case.
Is this a capital case ?
It was done in the Shortiss case.

The hanging of a man
is a serious matter, and a case that involves the whole future of the British Empire is of such a nature that confidence must be reposed in those who are in high authority. After consulting with those in charge of affairs in England, was the Prime Minister of Canada to come here and create a panic ? We all know that when the North Atlantic Trading Company frauds were exposed in this House a few years ago, and it was shown that hundreds of thousands of dollars had been illegally and improperly spent, the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) rose in his place and said, we cannot give the names of the parties involved because they will hang themselves; and yet hon. gentlemen opposite say that every confidence which was reposed in the Prime Minister of Canada by the lords of the Admiralty should be revealed to the people of Canada.
Let us take another case. There was a certain gentleman, the head of a great political party in this country, who went from one end of the Dominion to the other, sounding a note of alarm. Did he tell the people of Canada that his party was not going to succeed ? No, east and west, north and south, he told his friends; ' Put your money on the old cock,' and to-day the right hon. gentleman is cursed roundly by his friends and admirers who lost their money in betting on the old cock. It is absurd and preposterous to suggest that the secret and confidential matters that were arranged between the lords of the Admiralty and the Prime Minister of Canada and his colleagues, should be made public. Sympathetic meetings between the lords of the Admiralty and the representatives of Canada were held, and as a result this Bill is before the Parliament of Canada, and to a great extent it has the approval of the people of Canada. It is wonderful to listen to hon. gentlemen opposite in their at-temns to make merry over the question of agreement between Canada and Great Britain on this great question. speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The correction of the hon. gentleman does not at all come within the scope of the words which he uttered; but it does not matter. No resolutions were prepared, and we went to that meeting in the exercise of our rights as British-Canadian subjects to present our views to the people of Toronto.
I do not propose, Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the debate to go into the general discussion which has engaged the attention of the House now for many weeks. I do not know whether I shall be luckier than my hon. friend behind me, who just put a question to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister as to the very important amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) to clause 2.
But, before I approach this subject I desire to say a word in reply to the observation which has been heard several times during the last few days, as to the length of the debate upon this Bill in the committee stage. This observation was made as if implying that the length of the discussion had been abnormal and excessive. It has been stated frequently that the Bill has been in the committee stage now for twenty days. I ventured earlier in the day to say that this was neither abnormal nor
excessive, but that I could point out instances in England where, notwithstanding the gag, the guillotine and the kangaroo, which a member of this Government could pray God we should not have in this country-he will not be able to pray God any more-notwithstanding all these obstacles to free speech, the debates in the committee stage on one Bill occupied more than one, two, or three weeks. In these modern days the discussion of a Bill in committee is the important part of it; indeed, it is stated by authorities that the most important part of the consideration of a Bill has always been in the committee stage. The Austrian author, Redlieh, who has written on the British parliamentary system perhaps with greater clearness than any British writer, has this to say with reference to the discussion of a Bill in the Committee of the Whole:
We may, then, say that the centre of the whole legislative action of the House of Commons lies in the region of the work of Committee of the Whole House. It is in committee that the fate of a Bill is really decided; its ultimate form is there settled in the clash of parties and opinions or by the compromises made between them. In this stage debate is quite free; members may speak to each question as often as necessary. Speeches in committee are generally short, to the point, businesslike and simple. Their manner is almost conversational and seldom tinged with rhetoric. The object of committee debate is to arrive at decisions upon special questions of substance and to settle the essential points of detail one by one. The aim of what is said is to convince, not to gain a mere debating advantage. Committee therefore offers to individual members the best scope for display of expert knowledge, untiring industry, capacity for routine work and ready action; many a new member makes his reputation there, especially a man whose claims to foremost rank in Parliament are based upon ability and knowledge of political and administrative business rather than on brilliance of oratorical display. On a Bill of first rate importance the committee stage may last for weeks.
Everybody will agree that this, is a Bill of first rate importance, and therefore it i$ nothing unusual, nothing extraordinary, that the committee stage should have lasted weeks, as it has already. Indeed, the very observation which I have read from Redlieh is exemplified by a fact to which I desire to call the attention of the House. My hon. friend from Welland has proposed an amendment which goes to the root of this Bill, which is of extraordinary importance, which was introduced only two or three days ago, and which has not occupied more than a couple of hours discussion. The second clause of the Bill which we now have before us is in these terms :

Surely the right hon. gentleman remembers that those were Bills of a very lengthy character, with two hundred, three hundred or four hundred sections and involving complex considerations. It was upon Bills of that kind, not upon Bills of less than half a page in length, that two or three or four weeks have been taken in the Imperial Parliament, if my recollection is correct, and I think it is.
The right hon. gentleman has said that Parliament will have no account in respect of the payments made under an Act of this character, if passed by Parliament, until after every important step has been taken. Well, what fuller account was given to Parliament in respect of the ships my right hon. friend undertook to build in 1910? What fuller account is given in respect of any appropriation for the Transcontinental railway? What fuller account will be given upon the appropriation asked for by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways in respect of the enlargement of the Welland canal? We have given to this committee every information that is available for the purpose, and if hon. gentlemen on the other side have not received ail the information that should be given, it is because they have not asked lor it, but have occupied the time that should have been devoted to legitimate criticism of the Bill in committee, in carrying on a debate which should have been carried on upon the second reading of the Bill.
My right hon. friend in the ehd made three inquiries of me. He desires to know, in the first place, why it is that we do not assent to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German), which was supported by arguments -from that hon. gentleman, that an amendment should be made to the second section of this Bill which, in effect, would absolutely cut that clause out; it provides that $35,000,000 shall not be appropriated now but shall be appropriated whenever it is voted by Parliament. The situation would be exactly the same if section 2 as proposed by my hon. friend from Welland were not in the Bill at all, because it could not take effect until the appropriation was voted by Parliament.
And that is the very thing w-e are asking -that this sum for the purpose of rendering the immediate and effective aid to the Empire which we deem is necessary, shall be voted by Parliament here and now, in order that the Empire and the nations of the world shall know that Canada will

give this effective aid at this juncture. In what way is the public interest to be safeguarded by yearly appropriations, more than it is safeguarded by the proposals we lay before Parliament? Have we not given to the best of our ability all information asked for by hon. gentlemen on the other side-more than the right hon. gentleman himself gave in 1910 when he placed his proposal before Parliament? What is the effect of his proposal that we should emasculate this Bill by striking out that which alone makes it effective, the granting of the money? It is to hand what one might call a gold brick to the Mother Country in the shape of an empty measure that would not be effective until Parliament had further considered what appropriation should be made for it. The right hon. gentleman may consider that the best way of dealing with a great question of this character, but I am bound to say, so far a3 I am concerned, that his suggestion does not in the slightest degree commend itself to my judgment, if we are to assume -and the right hon. gentleman tells us that we ought to assume-that it is the desire of both sides of this House to do what is reasonable and necessary in the interest of the whole Empire at this time.

I am aware of that, but that is not the point with which I am dealing. I am asking why this particular provision, requiring the construction to be by tender and contract, was not attached to that appropriation. This is an appropriation of $35,000,000 for the construction of battleships; that was an appropriation of eight or ten millions for the construction of smaller ships, and there was no stipulation attached to that appropriation that these ships should be built by tender and contract. My right hon. friend very properly undertook to build them by tender, but he did not make any stipulation of that kind in connection with his appropriation Bill. The answer given to me across the floor of the House when I adduced that illustration in reply to the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German), was this: Oh, that was the Tegular appropriation bill, but this is not. If any member of this committee can see any reason or any sound argument in that distinction, he has a quality of intellect that I do not possess. If it is proper that we should have in this Bill a stipulation that these vessels must be built by tender and contract, then I say it will reasonably occur to every hon. member of this House, on this side or the Mr. BORDEN.
other side, that it would have been equally proper and necessary to have made such a provision in connection with the vote that the right hon. gentleman asked for in 1910. I challenge hon. gentlemen to indicate any possible distinction between the two cases. I have no desire or intention to depart from the ordinary procedure in this case; but, as I pointed out last night, it is possible that, if Parliament approves of this Bill, some of these ships may be built in one of the royal dockyards in Great Britain, in which case I assume they would not be built by tender and contract, but would be constructed under the close and vigilant supervision of the officials of the Admiralty in England. I said last night, and I repeat it now, that so far as the construction of these ships is concerned, we shall be governed by the advice of the Admiralty, who have had practical knowledge and experience in these matters which are not possessed in Canada by the Government or by any person in the employ of the Government.
My right hon. friend asks lastly whether or not we shall submit to Parliament the contracts and all information in connection with them. I say to my right hon. friend undoubtedly so, and all details of expenditure so far as they shall be available, I have already introduced an amendment to this Bill for that very purpose. This is an appropriation of public money, and it is not only eminently desirable but necessary tnat we should have in this Bill every possible safeguard for the public interests. After having been appropriated, the money is to be expended under the control of the Governor in Council, and upon the Governor in Council will rest the responsibility for the wise and prudent expenditure of that money, and of affording to this Parliament ail information in conection with it. It would be perfectly idle for this Government or for any government to seek to divest itself of any part of that responsibility, and we do not for one moment desire or intend to do so. i say again to my right hon. friend that we see no reason why the whole of this money should not be voted at once, in order that the construction of these ships may be assured once and for all. So far as the tenders are concerned, we propose to abide by the usage which has characterized the practice of Doth governments in that regard, subject to the consideration to which I have alluded-that some of these ships might be constructed in the Royal dockyards; and, so far, as information is concerned, we shall deem it our absolute duty to furnish all information in connection with the expenditure of this money that may be available to us.

course will be followed; I see no reason why it should not; but I have already given assurance to my hon. friend that so far as the construction of these ships is concerned we shall be guided by the advice and experience of those who know a great deal more about this kind of work than we do. It seems to me that that assurance ought to commend itself to every hon. gentleman in this House, and I hope that they will regard it as a reasonable statement of the position of the Government in this connection.
In conclusion, I can only say, Mr. Chairman, that having given this information io rny right hon. friend, I trust that I may have his support in the passage of this measure. He stated to the people of Ca ' ada, during his recent address at Toronto, and also in the early part of this session that he and his party are willing to make such provision as many be necessary for the purpose of giving at this juncture the desired aid in the defence of the whole Empire. This is not a question of the defence of Great Britain and the British Islands alone; it is not a question of the defence of that commerce and shipping which belongs exclusively to the United Kingdom. In making this provision we are primarily providing for the defence of Canadian commerce and Canadian shipping, because that commerce and that shipping and the defence of our interests upon the high seas can be fully and absolutely safeguarded only by the protection of all the naval forces of the Empire. In assisting the naval forces of the Empire at a time when help seems very much needed, we should not regard that assistance as some hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have been inclined to look at it- as aid sent by Canada for the advantage and benefit of people in the British Isles alone. It is not in that spirit that this measure is being proposed, because we have declared that these ships are to be placed at the disposal of His Majesty the King for the common defence of the whole Empire. It is for the common defence of the whole Empire that we ask the co-operation of our hon. friends on the other side *of the House, and I trust that, in the end, they may come to the conclusion that, however much they may criticise some aspects of the proposal, yet in its largest and broadest and widest aspects, it is one that commends itself to their judgment, and that the purpose of the measure, if not all its methods and details, they are prepared to support and to assist us in carrying it out.
I realize to the full, Mr. Chairman, what was alluded to by rny hon. friend for South Eenfrew (Mr. Graham) last evening, that it is unfortunate that there has been a divergence of views between the two parlies in this respect; but, for the purpose 302
of endeavouring to convince my hon. friends on the other side of the ' House,
I pointed out some weeks ago that even if this measure passed, these ships could not be put in - commission until after a general election had been held in this country, and if, as my hon. friends have so often and loudly boasted, the people of Canada are of the opinion that their proposals are those upon which this country should embark, then it is absolutely possible for this measure to pass, for this money to be voted, for these ships to be built, and for the proposals which my hon. friends on the other side of the House favour to be carried out. The determined and defiant opposition which is offered to this Bill I am absolutely unable to under-'d, and I trust that, in view of the ex- ' -.-ion I have given to-night, and of the suggestion which I have just now made, hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House will, in the end, join with us in putting this measure through, and in doing something effective and necessary for the common defence of the Empire 'of which we form a part.
Mr. Chairman, we have listened with considerable interest-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I would certainly
allow the hon. gentleman all the time he deserves.

We have listened with considerable interest to the remarks of the right hon. the Prime Minister. I am sure that we have made some progress this evening, and had we a few more days' discussion on this measure, we might be greatly enlightened. The right hon. gentleman _ has _ spoken of what he styled a little Bill with a few sections. It is a little Bill with a few sections, and, on account of its length, ought not to require a great deal of discussion. But my right hon. friend will admit that its import is very great for the British Empire, and for the Dominion of Canada. Where my hon. friend makes a mistake is in saying that he thinks the Opposition wished to introduce certain amendments in order to have him send these ships over to England as a gold brick. My conception of a gold brick is something which



is gilded on the outside, and which contains none of the precious metal within. As I heard the right hon. gentleman speak of these ships being sent over as a gold brick. I thought that, in their present form, they answered the exact definition of a gold brick, something precious on the outside, but containing absolutely nothing within. And when the right hon. gentleman came to his final plea, and said what he has said on several occasions, _ that the ships cannot be placed in commission before an election takes place, I think he used the weakest of all the arguments which he has placed before the House, and if the right hon. gentleman would permit me to say so,
I must give him credit for having used very powerful arguments in advocating at least some policy which would be in the interests of the "British Empire. But let me call the right hon. gentleman's attention to the point at issue. It is not so much the sending of the ships, .as the mode of expenditure of the money, that is the point at issue. The right hon. gentleman has said that he has power under the constitutional law to ask this Parliament for a certain sum of money, and to send that money over to Great Britain without Parliament knowing the conditions and terms of the expenditure. I will refeT in a moment to certain sections of this Bill to prove to the right hon. gentleman that if the Bill is passed in its present form he has absolutely no power, and this Parliament has no power to make any conditions, to impose any terms, or to make any arrangements with the Government of Great Britain, unless the Government of Great Britain sees fit to make such terms or arrangements. Before 1 come to that point, I would like to point out to the committee that when the right hon. the leader of the Opposition was arguing that this House has a right to know just how the money was expended, he was following out exactly terms of the contract entered into by the late Government^ which contracts were subject to ratification by this Parliament. The rule which is laid down in Todd's Parliamentary Government in England, as found on page 489 of the second edition, is as follows:
Furthermore, that if any contract he entered into by any executive department for work to he performed, the cost of which will exceed the amount already voted by Parliament for the service to be contracted for, such contract should expressly state that payments on behalf of the same would be made ' out of moneys to be voted by Parliament;' and that application should be made to Parliament for a further appropriation to cover such increase of expenditure. This would afford an opportunity to the House of Commons to express its disapproval of the matter, if it should think fit to do so.
The course which was followed by the late Government, and which the right hon.
Mr. DEVLIN.
the leader of the Opposition is asking the Prime Minister to follow out in this instance, is the course which should be followed under the authority of the constitutional law of this country and of Great Britain. The question which is immediately under consideration in clause 2, is not so much the disposition to be made of the ships, as the mode of expenditure. Let me read this clause;
From out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada, there may be paid and applied a sum not exceeding $35,000,000 for the purpose of immediately increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire.
Will the right hon. the Prime Minister allow me to ask him one question for information? Under the Bill, $35,000,000 are to be voted by this Parliament for one purpose and one purpose only, that of building three ships. Under section 3 the money is to be expended on the construction and equipment of battleships or armoured cruisers of the most modern and powerful type. Under section 4 they must automatically go to the British Empire. The wording is:
Shall said ships when constructed and equipped he placed by the Governor in Council at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of the Empire.
The moment his ships are built they must automatically go over to . Great Britain for the common defence of the Empire. Under what authority can he make ' terms, conditions and arrangements ' with Great Britain ? If the wording of section 5:
Subject to such terms, conditions and arrangements as. may he agreed upon between the Governor in Council and His Majesty's Government.
-were immediately after the words contained in section 4, and formed part of section 4, he could make terms and arrangements with Great Britain. But clause 4 stands by itself, it is a law in itself, and it says that the Government must place these ships at the disposal of Great Britain. If Great Britain refuses to make terms, conditions and arrangements, suitable to the Canadian Government, what action can my right hon. friend or his Government take ? Would he give me an answer to that question ? I do not say that they will refuse, but if they should refuse.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The British Admiralty
have already signified their willingness to accept the ships, and the terms and conditions have, in the broad sense, already been communicated to this House. The hon. gentleman surely understands, from his knowledge and experience as an eminent member of the Bar, that sections 4 and 5 must be read together.

I understand the right
hon. gentleman's point, but I am asking him a direct question. If the Government of Great Britain refuses to make terms and conditions suitable to the Government of Canada-these ships then are built.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken about that; the ships are not built.

But the moment the
ships are built, they must, under section 4, go over to Great Britain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The money shall be
used and applied to build ships, and the ships shall be constructed and placed at the disposal of 'His Majesty, subject to such terms, conditions and arrangements as may be agreed upon between the Governor in Council and His Majesty's Government.
By section 4.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
think there is any difficulty about the making of these arrangements before the contracts were let or before the order is given to construct the ships in the dockyard ?
But we are in committee at the present time, and one of the duties of the committee is to consider the wording of the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Quite so; absolutely
right.

Under the wording of this Bill my right hon. friend must place these ships automatically at the disposal of the British Government; so says section 4. Section 5 gives him the power to make terms and conditions with the British Government. But if the British Government offer terms and conditions which are not acceptable to my right hon. friend, the $35,000,000 is voted and, under the law, it must be applied to the construction of the ships. Your ships are constructed and automatically they must go to Great Britain. What terms and conditions can you make F

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that I can make it plain to my hon. friend; I will try once more. The terms, conditions and arrangements are to be agreed upon under section 5.

Why was that not placed under section 4?
_ Mr. BORDEN:	Will my hon. friend
'pardon me; he is too eager. If we do not get the terms, conditions and arrangements satisfactorily settled, we are not obliged to build the ships.

That is a new phase of the question altogether.
