speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a very old
phase to me.

Then this is not a free
gift; it is not a contribution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have explained to my hon. friend and to other members of the committee a great many times that the ships are to be under the ownership of Canada and that they are to be placed at the disposal of His Majesty for the common defence of the Empire. I have also explained that if these ships are required for a Canadian navy, or for a Canadian division of the British navy, or a Canadian unit of an Imperial navy, they may be recalled upon reasonable notice.
You have not that power under the law as it stands to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think so.

My hon. friend has introduced a new phase of the question. We are getting some information now. We started upon the consideration of this question with the booming of cannons and the holding of tremendous receptions. The right hon. gentleman had come back from Great Britain and announced that he was going to make a great big free contribution to Great Britain for the defence of the Empire. I presume that was a sentiment that was acceptable to Great Britain and Canada. We afterwards heard that there was an emergency threatening Great Britain and that on account of that emergency we should spend $35,000,000 for three ships to be put at the disposal of the British navy. We also later heard that the British Admiralty had prepared a memorandum. After reading that memorandum my right hon. friend came to the conclusion that the only dignified action for this country to take was to send $35,000,000 over to Great Britain. We heard to-night for the first time from the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett)- I noted his words-a new explanation. His explanation was that there was a sympathetic meeting between representatives of Great Britain and Canada with this Bill as a result. He thought that this sympathetic meeting between the representatives of Canada and Great Britain, and a certain degree of sentiment, were the causes of this Bill coming before the Canadian Parliament. When he said that, the thought which passed through my mind was that, if it was due to a sympathetic meeting between representatives of Great Britain and Canada, and if it was due to a certain amount of sentiment, what becomes of my right hon. friend's argument earlier in the session that he based the whole of his policy upon the memorandum of the Board of Admiralty? What becomes of the argument that we have heard

so often that even if the British Admiralty had never prepared the memorandum, there was a great big emergency facing the British Empire? There was war over in the Balkans, there was war all around us and therefore we had to run to Great Britain with $35,000,000. My right hon. friend said last night that he was guided a great deal by sentiment. I am speaking purely and simply as a Canadian, and as one belonging to a country within the British Empire, intent upon doing all he can to strengthen the bonds of the British Empire but whose first duty is to his own country. I have tried to get as much education upon this question as possible.
I started back to ,1909 and my eyes first fell upon an article published in the University Magazine, which is under the editorial supervision of such distinguished gentlemen as W. Peterson, M.A., C.M.G., LL.D., principal; P. P. Walton, LL.D., dean, Faculty of Law, McGill University; W. J. Alexander, B.A., Ph.D., professor of English; Pelham Edgar, Ph.D., professor of French; J. Mavor, professor of Political Economy, University of Toronto; Archibald McMeehen, B.A., Ph.D., professor of English, Dal-housie College, Halifax. I assume that any article which would have been submitted to this editorial committee dealing with a matter connected with the British Empire would have the right ring about it, and that if I followed the principles therein enumerated I would be pursuing a sound course. The purpose of the University Magazine, as set forth on the title page is: ' To express an educated opinion upon questions immediately concerning Canada,' and the very first article in this magazine is upon the Canadian navy. The article which is published under the supervision of these eminent Empire builders says:
One thing I shall take for granted. It must be a naval force of onr own. The proposal that we pay a cash contribution to the Royal navy-let our defence out to contract, hire Englishmen to do our maritime fighting for us-has been discussed; and I think that the sense of the nation has turned decisively against it
Seeing that article was exactly in line with the policy laid down by my right hon. leader

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The time of the hon. gentleman has expired.
I had a great deal to say had I more time, but I must submit to the rules, although I would like to finish the reading of this article.
Go on.

The article continues to
say:
Thus it seems suitable that our naval
force should be devoted at the outset to coastal defence. We should guard our coasts so well that no enemy's cruiser would care Mr. DEVLIN.
to haunt them, and that our ships sailing to England, could gain the blue water without molestation. Later, when our_ coastal defence is organized, we may consider the advisability of discouraging hostile cruisers from hanging about in the North Atlantic; but that is matter for a fairly distant future.
This article practically winds up with the significant words:
Meanwhile, our Canadian Government could be acquiring the ships-gun-vessels, small cruisers, big cruisers, torpedo craft, submarines-as the progress of the service rendered necessary, and could be building upon the shore establishments which go with ships. The ownership of the material should be strictly Canadian.
Which means, of course, that the navy should be built in Canada. I find that this article is signed by one C. Frederick Hamilton, and not knowing who the gentleman was I made some inquiry and learned that it was he who inspires for the Toronto News all items that go out from this House. If my right hon. friend the Prime Minister wants us to be educated upon the question, he cannot ask us to go to a hotter source than the authority of Mr. Frederick Hamilton. Before resuming my seat, Mr. Chairman, I would like to call the attention of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) to the fact that when he says the Prime Minister has been consistent in his naval attitude, he is making a great big, well I shall say statement-that I think is parliamentary-but it is rather difficult to find parliamentary language to characterize the assertion made by the hon. member (Mr. Bennett). I have been partly educated on this question by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, and I find that speaking in the city of Halifax where shipbuilding was once a great industry, the right hon. gentleman lauded the Laurier Naval Service Bill of 1909 and stated it would revive the ancient industry of shipbuilding in Halifax. I was curious to know what that ship-building has been of which my right hon. friend had spoken, and I asked the Government a question about it some time ago, but I have not yet got the information. However, I will call the attention of the Prime Minister to some interesting reading in the work of Mr. Castell Hopkins who informs us that up to the time of the abrogation of the reciprocity treaty in 1866, the ship-building industry of Canada was considerable, but the moment that reciprocity treaty was abrogated, ship-building declined in Nova Scotia and elsewhere. Air. Hopkins says:
There were several other vessels equally remarkable. The ship-builders in Quebec hastened to build for the United States markets prior to the expiration of the reciprocity treaty but this abrogation of the arrangement and the sudden demand for iron ships reduced ship-building there as elsewhere in British America to its lowest ebb.

There was a ship-building industry in Nova Scotia, Mr. Hopkins tells us:
In 1850 the largest ship that went up the Clyde was built in Nova Scotia and Nova Scotia was then the leading province in Confederation in ship-building.
I feel that if I went on giving this information to the committee which the Government has failed to give me, I would be exceeding the limits of the time at my disposal under the new rule.
I certainly do not wish to be qualified as an obstructionist or as breaking rules, whether I consider those rules justly or wisely passed, wise or unwise. As long as I have a seat in this House, I for one shall try to respect the authority of Parliament.
Before I resume my seat, I should like to say that, if it had not been for the gag, I would like to have taken up the report of the conference dealing with the military and naval defence of the Empire, and to have asked my right hon. friend a number of questions. I also wanted to take up speeches which have been made by the right hon. the Prime Minister in Great Britain, wherein he said that the autonomy of the Dominion should be safeguarded in all matters of self-defence.
Time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Goon.

Who leads? Does my
right hon. friend lead, or do those behind him lead? The majority, we are told, must rule in this House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend is leading the House.
My right hon. friend is in the minority. I must bow to the rule of the majority behind him, who insist upon my resuming my seat.

Mr. Chairman, in considering the amendments to section 2, which I understand are before the committee, I desire to say that I strongly support, especially the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. * German), requiring that the money which is to provide the proposed naval aid to the Empire shall be voted by Parliament. I do so because it is the rule of Parliament, it is the first principle of parliamentary government that, in the granting or voting of estimates, there is the right on the part of Parliament to the fullest possible information from the Government in regard to the purposes for which this money is to be used, the reason for the proposal being made and the expected consequences of the payment.
I disagree entirely with the position taken by the Prime Minister that there has been
exhaustive information given by the Government in regard to the subject matter of this Bill. When he suggests that because the Bill contains only six clauses, therefore it is not properly a subject for long or serious discussion, or properly a subject for the asking and answering of great, important and many questions, I can only say that I do not agree with him. I maintain that the mechanical fact of a Bill containing only six clauses has no bearing whatever on the importance of the measure, of the questions involved in it, or of the right of Parliament to know from the Government every particular in regard to the questions so involved. When the right hon. the Premier suggests to Parliament and to the country that there has been obstruction of this measure by Teason of the attitude of the Opposition, I want to say emphatically that such obstruction or such delay, as this measure has met with in reaching its present stage, is solely and only because the Government of the day absolutely refused on their own behalf to give the information that this House and country was entitled to, and refused their followers the privilege of giving their opinions in regard to the measure.
When my right hon. friend presented his resolution to the House, he raised a number of questions, giving reasons why this proposal of his was a good ofie. I maintain that the House is entitled to know just what merit there, was in each one of those reasons. He said that this measure would be the beginning of the establishment of a shipbuilding industry in Canada. He had made arrangements with the British Admiralty whereby they would undertake the construction of vessels in Canada, subject to Canada paying the difference in the cost between Canadian construction and British construction. A great part of the contention of the Liberal party has been in regard to the question of construction in Canada. My hon. friend, from the moment that the last word of the paragraph in his speech to which I have just alluded left his lips, has never since alluded to that suggestion which he placed before Parliament as one reason why this proposal should be passed, and none of his followers have done so. The House had a right to know how far this proposed system of construction was likely, to be carried. He said that if we voted this money, under the conditions that he proposed, protection would be given to our Pacific coast by the British fleet, such as it does not receive at the present time, that is to say, that the proposal placed before Parliament by the Opposition for the maintenance of a Canadian fleet unit on both coasts was rendered unnecessary by the arrangement

that he had with the British Admiralty. He has given no word of information in regard to that matter. Nearly half of the speech he made on that occasion was devoted to a statement that the principle of his Government was that there should not be naval aid to Britain unless there was control in Canada. He has given no further information in regard to the important proposal for a change in the constitutional relationship between Canada and the United Kingdom in connection with this measure. And when all these points have been discussed from this side of the House, when questions have been asked by the Ministry, they have been addressed to empty ministerial benches. The Government has not done this House the courtesy to sit in tlieir places and be prepared, or be willing, to answer the questions that were addressed to them. Not only so, but, as I said, they denied to their followers the privilege of even voicing their opinions. My right hon. friend has said that they gave information. They gave information? The information they gave-I will not use stronger language-is yet the subject of controversy in this House as to its accuracy. And they only condescended to profess to give information, if my memory is right, during a period of some three hours during which section 2 of the Bill came under discussion in Committee of the Whole, until they entered upon the policy of undertaking to conduct the business of Parliament by the rule of physical force. Since that time they have not condescended to give this House one atom of information in regard to the subject matter of section 2 of the Bill. If there has been delay in the carrying forward of this measure, I want the House and the country to understand that the delay is because of the action of the Government, it is because of the assertion by the Opposition of the right of the people of Canada to have the fullest particulars in regard to the policy of the Government on this important question. My right hon. friend, when challenged with the demand that Parliament should vote this money from year to year and thereby be in a position to demand particulars of its uses and expenditure, has said that it was important under the conditions existing that there should be an announcement made to the world that Canada was prepared to vote $35,000,000. When he said that, he said it with the intention of creating the impression in the country that this vote was to be a strength to the Empire, that it was to have a practical and immediate result. I say, he wanted to create that impression. But in the course of this debate, whether it has lasted one month or three months, he has never yet put into words anything that would bind himself or his Government to any definite action at any Mr. OLIVER.
time towards the strengthening of the Empire in any practical way by the use of this money. There have been evidences of these conditions brought to the attention of the House before, but I propose to take the liberty of bringing again before the House the evidence that in the minds of some of the right hon. gentleman's^ supporters, what he said in this House did not convey the idea that he desired to convey to the country. And they are absolutely close to the ear of my right hon. friend, members of his Government, associates of his in Parliament-they hold views such as I will quote to the House. I read from La Semaine, published in Grand Mbre, Champlain county, of the issue of Friday, May 2:
Last Scruples-Opposition to a Moral Aid has no Sense-Neither has a referendum.
The idea of a Canadian navy, the phantom of periodical contributions, the assailamts who might prey on our cheese and butter on the high seas, as well as the famous so-called gift of thirty-five millions, are so many ruses made up for the fight; but documents, reasons and common sense have already triumphed over them all. It has now been admitted even by the Opposition, that the Borden proposals mean none of these. They amount purely and simply to a demonstration of friendship which cannot take, until many years, any other form but that of a moral aid; at least as long as the people will not have been consulted.
Does the committee remember that on the 5th of December last, when my right hon. friend was shaking with fear at the sound of the thunder and the flashes of the lightnings of war, he demanded then that $35,000,000 should be voted as an emergency towards the Empire? But here on the 2nd of May a reputable newspaper, representing the sentiments held by the supporters of my right hon. friend in the county of Champlain, says the proposals mean a demonstration of friendship which cannot take, until many years, any other form than that of moral aid.
The article goes on;
The Borden contribution was formerly declared by the Quebec Conservatives to be no less nefarious than the Laurier navy. One must not forget that that contribution meant the immediate gift of a sum of money from hand to hand to the Admiralty. It was a gift pure and simple. The present Bill mentions no gift; it provides for the construction in two or three years' time of three Canadian vessels which may be loaned to England in five or six years' time. It bears no resemblance -whatsoever to the Borden proposal when made by him in opposition. There is no more talk of contribution. This Bill only lends a moral help to England, and safeguards the rights of the Canadian people.
The article goes on:
As a premature, if not useless, Canadian navy and a passive contribution without any

condition, the, Conservative party has selected the most happy solution. A loan which give a moral aid in the eyes of the world, and which in the last resort reserves to the people the supreme decision.
With such statements as these presented as being the mind of a large and important section of the supporters of the right hon. gentleman in regard to this proposal, which he represented to the people of Canada! in an entirely different light, this opposition is and has been more than justified by every moment of the delay that has occurred in bringing to a conclusion the discussion in regard to this measure. My hon. friend has insulted Parliament by refusing to give the information to which Parliament is entitled, as he has insulted Canada by asking Parliament to consent to a proposal that brands Canadians as cowards, and denies to the Empire that help and that assistance to which it is entitled, and which Canada and Canadians are and always have been proud to render.
Hon. RODOT/PHE LEMIEUX: I had no intention of taking part in this debate, as I have spoken before on different occasions; but my right hon. friend the leader of the House, doubtless without wishing to impugn my good faith in the administration of the department which was under my cara when I was a member of the Government, said a moment ago that I had departed from the golden rule provided under the constitution of making yearly appropriations for the expenditure of public money.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I said my hon. friend
had entered into a contract extending over a period of twenty years.

If my hon. friend refers to the stamp-vending machines, which are now in use in this Dominion, in hotels, post offices and lumber camps, he is about right; but I beg to inform him that this was done with the knowledge of the Parliament of Canada. It was not done secretly, and without the consent of the House of Commons and the Governor General. During the session of 1911 I introduced legislation which my hon. friend will find in 1 and 2 George V, chapter 19, intituled an Act to Amend the Post Office Act. This legislation was introduced during the session of 1911, and my right hon. friend will find in ' Hansard,' session 1910-11, volume 5, pages 8065, 8066 and following pages, the necessary explanation as to that legislation. My hon. friend was in his seat at the time, because I notice that I addressed myself to him whilst I was explaining the Bill. I said for instance:
As my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition is aware, the postal box in the street
is, according to the Post Office Act, a post office by itself.
This new device was placed in post offices, lumber camps and large hotels, so that on Sundays and local holidays the people of the hotels and in these camps would get their stamps without going to the post offices. In introducing this Bill, I said:
The stamp vending boxes can be purchased by the department, and placed here and there in the country; we have already purchased 50 as a trial, but our inspectors, and our superintendent of post offices, Mr. Ross, state that in certain sections of the country, especially where we have lumber camps, we may have difficulty in getting a regular post office, or even a regular agent for the sale of stamps to lumbermen. My officers say that we might well give the company which manufactures the boxes the privilege of installing those boxes in those remote sections of the country, the company to draw what commission we would pay to agents having 6tamp vending licenses.
That is the gist of the legislation concerning the stamp vending machines. I have no recollection of a coimact which was passed with the company, but even if the contract was passed -

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think the contract was made first with an individual, and then transferred to a company.

At all events, I would like my hon. friend to think that he does not find anything improper in the contract, because no money was paid to the company that obtained the license; they got the commission which any licensee would have received.
I gave a full explanation to the House at the time the Bill was introduced. The device, which had been adopted in England and in Australia, was called a conscience box, because no false coins could be introduced into it. All I have to say is that I got authority from Parliament, and that any contracts which might have been entered into by officers of the department with the company were proper contracts and in the interests of the service.
Now, to come back to the question which occupies the attention of the House. I have listened with great pleasure to the speech made this afternoon by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames). It is many weeks ago since we heard from the hon. gentleman. I do not know in what spirit he read the statement made only yesterday in the British House of Commons by the Colonial Secretary on his pet scheme of Imperial federation. When in December or January last the hon. gentleman delivered his very interesting speech in this House, he stated that, in his judgment, the days of autonomy were gone, and that now Canada should think imperially; that is to

say, should seek Imperial federation. I listened with great attention to the weighty remarks made at that time by the hon. gentleman, but he will find in this morning's Citizen an announcement which may alter his mind as regards that Imperial scheme of his.
Regarding Imperial federation, Hon. Mr. Harcourt said he wanted clear information. Was the parliament to be elective? If so, was it to be on the basis of population? Or area? Or what was it to be on ? On white population alone? Was it to have supreme legislative or taxation powers?
I will not quote the balance of the remarks made by Mr. Harcourt. Only an Englishman from England could use the language attributed to him. If a humble Colonial, belonging to the minority, as myself, were perchance to refer to the tea-chest party, I would at once be branded as a traitor and a separatist. But, reverting to the statement made by Mr. Harcourt, what will the Imperial Parliament be ? Will it be based on the population of the United Kingdom and the colonies; will it be based on colour, or on area ? What will be the legislation framed and enacted by that Parliament ? With the keen common sense of John Bull, Mr. Harcourt has expressed in three lines all the objections which have been found insuperable for the last thirty or forty years.
The hon. member for St. Antoine has referred with great gusto to the programme published by the Australian Commonwealth on the occasion of the arrival in Australian waters of His Majesty's ship Melbourne, and he thought he had made a point when he read from that programme the statement that the Melbourne had been practically designed and built in Great Britain. Who has ever said that the first ships of the Canadian units would be built in Canada ? The right hon. leader of the Opposition, and every hon. member on this side of the House know well, that Canada cannot now begin to build dreadnoughts. But can we not imitate the action of Australia by starting with British firms, and inducing those British firms to do in Canada what they are doing in Australia, what they have done in Italy, and what they are doing in Spain to-day? The hon. gentleman quoted but one passage from that souvenir programme; he should have turned the page and read to this House the words of the Minister of Defence, the Hon. Mr. Pearce. They are there on the programme as a lesson to be remembered by the children and grand-children of those Who witnessed the demonstration in Australian waters. Let me quote the words of the Australian Minister of Defence:
We in Australia feel that we have reached manhood, and that the grown-up son should shoulder some of the great responsibility Mr. LEMIEUX.
which the parent nation ha^ been carrying so long and so nobly.
These are the sentiments of the truly loyal Canadians who advocate the creation of a Canadian navy.	*
The arrival of the Melbourne is a concrete illustration of the national awakening. What we are doing to-day and what is planned for
the future must have regard to the possibilities of the morrow. The British Empire is one, and the fleets of the Empire must have one common object and be able to work together in every emergency. The duty which lies nearest our doors is the protection of British interests in the Pacific. If we can maintain those interests in that ocean, we shall be doing something worthy of our history, and of service to the Empire and the commonwealth.
I say, Mr. Chairman, that we can well afford to duplicate what has been done by the sister dominion, the great Commonwealth of Australia. By duplicating the noble work of Australia we would be working, not only in the interests of this Dominion, but in the real interests of the British Empire. South Africa is to-day facing the same problem as that which has been faced by Australia, New Zealand and Canada. Not later than yesterday I read the words of the Prime Minister of South Africa who spoke on a resolution, introduced in the South African Parliament by one of the members of that House, favouring the policy which is being enacted here. General Botha stated that South Africa understood her duties by the Empire and by South Africa too, and that in his judgment, and in the judgment of the people of South Africa, the best policy was not one of contribution but the creation of a South African navy such as the Australian and New Zealand navies. We are told that the Malay States have offered to the Mother Country ships which, in the squadron stationed at Gibraltar, will be sister ships to those provided by Canada. If what I have read in the British papers is true, the gift of the Malay States is far from being a gift. I have read the story of that gift in the Referee of March 2, a paper published in London and, it looks .as if a large amount had been tolled from the semi-barbarian people of the Malay States.
Says the writer:
The * gift ' of a battleship is no gift. It is an exaction. It is a tribute. It is a levy of ship-money of the odious kind that was resisted by Hampden and I'ym in Stuart days. Memories are short. People forget what ship-mony is. A clever lawyer-placeman whispered to Charles the First that the equipment of ships should be levied from the roast towns. A writ for the money was issued. Next year a second writ was issued by which the inland towns and counties were required to contribute. Writ after writ was issued until the sum of four thousand five hundred

pounds was at last demanded from the county of Buckinghamshire to build a ship of 150 tons for use against the Scotch, with whom we were then at war. The levy of ship-money was pronounced illegal by the House of Lords (now abolished) in 1611. It is unseemly that the levy should be furtively revived at a great distance from these shores under circumstances of secrecy and tyranny that recall the Stuarts and their lawyers. We must give back that ship or pay for it ourselves.
Sir, let me say in conclusion that though the right hon. gentleman and his friends behind him may belittle the idea of a Canadian navy, though they may minimize the project, yet, to the minds and imaginations of the Canadian people, that project, that Canadian navy, appeals far more than the policy of tribute which is now being forced upon this Parliament. I do not forget the line which I read in a French poet: ' Mon verre n'est pas grand, mais je bois dans mon verre'-my glass is not large, but I drink in my glass. Our navy may not be a big navy, but it is a Canadian navy, in which we all have a deep interest. That Canadian navy project was endorsed first by our Parliament in 1910, then by the Home authorities in 1911. Our plain duty is to live up to the agreement which was passed between the Canadian Government and the Australasian Commonwealth at the last Imperial Conference.

Mr. Chairman, my object in rising is^to direct the attention of the committee to a very important admission made by the hon. mem/ber for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux). He stated in his remarks that Canada could not now build cruisers.

Not before having a
shipyard.

He stated most emphatically that Canada was not now in a position to build cruisers. What have we been fighting here since the 5th day of December? What has been the contention of the Opposition in this debate?-that Canada could build all the dreadnoughts and cruisers which were required for the defence of the country and of the Empire. But, at the end of this debate', a few minutes before the guillotine will be applied, we find this important admission made by a former minister of the Crown. What has been the argument of these hon. gentleman day and night almost since this debate began? The most important argument which these hon. gentlemen have adduced before the House and the country has been that Canada should build the ships for the protection of the Empire and that it was not necessary at all to pass this law which the Government has introduced in pursuance of an agreement with the British Admiralty. These remarks have been made by these gentlemen day in and day out since the 5th of December and now they are admitted to have been made for no use whatever, that they were futile and that they had no effect. They say now that we cannot build any ships until we get shipyards. What is the cost of the shipyards that they were going to build? When could these shipyards be completed? Could they equip these shipyards in a year, or two years or three years? When would these ships, which we require to-day for the defence of our country, be constructed? I think the statement made ,by the right hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Borden) is absolutely correct that it would take at least twenty-five years to put Canada in a position to be able to supply this country with a proper equipment to build these ships. Where would you get the men? We have not the workmen in this country to construct these ships. We would have to import them and before we could get any ships built, before we could put ourselves in a position to defend our country and our trade, we might find the great nations of Europe at one another's throats and we might probably find that Great Britain 'had fallen owing to the neglect of Canada to do her duty by the Empire. These admissions are made to-night in cool blood. The remarks prior to this were made very vehemently by members of the Opposition during the twelve days of continuous sitting. But to-night -we find these hon. gentlemen very quiet, a change has come over the spirit of their dreams. One says that we have no rules at all. One member of the late Administration, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), comes here and makes the bold statement that we have no rules and that we are simply at the mercy of the Opposition. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) stands up and says that he does not agree with the hon. member for St. John. I think we have a divided party. The man who led the House during the twelve days that the rumpus took place is now turned down by the member for Red Deer and we have the spectacle in this Parliament of two leading men who led that opposition to the naval project of the Prime Minister fighting amongst themselves. We know, and the members of the Opposition know themselves, that their arguments do not amount to anything. They had to put up some bluff before the country and one of their bluffs was the statement that we could build these ships in Canada. To-night we find them denuded of that argument, and nothing is left to them now except that they came here tonight, as they have come here many other nights and worked up the old threadbare argument that we should submit this question to the people of Canada. Did they sub-

mit the Naval Act of 1910 to the people of Canada? Was there one word uttered then by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in favour of submitting his Bill to the people? We all know that their contention in this respect is insincere. I do not believe they want the question submitted to the people. I do not believe there is a man who has studied this question from one end of Canada to the other who believes that the Liberals would have any chance in an election. They do not believe themselves they would succeed in an election, and they simply put up this bluff
Let us try.

These gentlemen tell the people of the country that if they got an election they would be returned to power, but what would they do if they were returned to power? I presume they would take up the old threadbare naval policy of 1910 and dilly-dally along with that and do nothing effective for the defence of the Empire. Why are 5,000,000 men under arms in Europe to-day? Suppose a conflict took place, the British navy would be employed defending the shores of Britain and what would become of the protection of our trade routes. We would have nothing to defend us.
Hear, hear.

I do not know what the hon. gentlemen are making so much noise about; their argument is all noise, all wind and nothing else, I heard a man in the corridor say to-night that the present position of the Opposition reminds him very much of the Scotchman who was playing the bagpipes and there was a lot of wind while the bag was full, but when the bag was pierced there was nothing left but the chanter. So it is with hon. gentlemen opposite: there is nothing left but shout in them to-night, and notwithstanding that they were so fond of blowing a few days ago.
The Argentine Republic is a country almost as rich as Canada, and the Argentine Republic is having its ships built in foreign countries for the simple reason that it is not in a position to erect shipyards at home. Australia and New Zealand are having their big ships built in England. These dominions are pursuing a common sense policy, and yet hon. gentlemen opposite who proclaim that they are so willing to take part in the defences of the Empire, set up the bluff that the ships should be built in Canada and not in England, when they know very well that if that policy were followed there would be no ships built in Canada for years and years to come, and no defence for the Empire. Their reasons against the policy proposed by the Prime Minister are Mr. McLEAN (Queens, P.E.I.)
without foundation and illogical. It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to make any extended remarks to-night, further than to draw attention to the fact that the hon. member for Rouville has receded from the position he and his friends took at the commencement of this debate.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a curious spectacle presented to this committee for the last two days, in that when hon. gentlemen opposite found that as the result of their closure measure the mouths of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House were to be definitely and certainly closed at a fixed hour, they immediately began to give utterance to all their thoughts and ideas which have been under absolute subjection ever since this measure was introduced on the 5th of December last. The illuminating propositions that have come from hon. gentlemen supporting the Government this afternoon, have been such as to indicate beyond a shadow of doubt that these gentlemen sadly needed instruction on the question. If any justification were required for the debate which has been carried on on this side of the House, it is to be found in the curious and wonderful speeches delivered by hon. gentlemen opposite this afternoon, because almost every one of them who spoke showed a total and absolute ignorance of the real issues, even as they had been stated by their own leaders. One hon. gentleman talked about this being a free gift to the Mother Country, when the Prime Minister himself has declared that that is not so. What is it a gift of? Is it a gift of money? No. Is it a gift of ships? No, because not a single ship is given to England. These hon. gentlemen opposite who sailed into beautiful adulations about the British Empire and the aid that was going to be given by the gift of these ships, talked about something that was absolutely incorrect. Other hon. gentlemen talked about the wonderful assistance that was going to be given to England because of this peculiar compromise between the Nationalists of Quebec and the Conservatives. Had these gentlemen listened to the speeches delivered on this side of the House they would not be in the humiliating position they found themselves in this afternoon. For example, the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) stated on the strength of an article in the National Review that Australia proposed to build something like fifty-two ships within the next twenty-two years, and he drew the inference that Australia was giving real aid to the Mother Country while the Liberal party in Canada hesitated to follow her example. But, it never dawned upon the hon. member (Mr. Cockshutt) that the naval law of the Commonwealth of Australia is almost word for word the Naval Ser-

vice Act of the Liberal party of 1910. Whatever Australia has done up to this date or may do in the future, it will be done under the law, the very principle of which was placed upon the statute book of the country in 1910. Let me read the report of Admiral Henderson who had come out from England to Australia to lead Australia along the proper path. It is absolutely conclusive evidence as to what Admiral Henderson's opinion is about the policy of South Africa and Australia in comparison with the know-nothing, no-name policy of the Conservative party in Canada. This is what Admiral Henderson said:
What paper?
A telegraphic despatch to the Manitoba Free Press.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If my hon. friend reads the context, he will see that I was not dealing with shipbuilding, but with the establishment of a naval organization.

My right hon. friend surely does not mean that he was referring to some peculiar naval organization in which there were to be no ships. This naval organization of the mysterious and peculiar character, that it was to take at least a quarter of a century to build up here, surely required the construction of some vessels. My right hon. friend is drawing too fine a distinction when he endeavours to escape from the positive statement that he made to this country when he introduced the measure, which statement has been heralded all over the country by his followers as a statement of fact. What is a naval organization? Is it an admiral, a commander, a group of clerks or officials in an office, or is it actual ships in which there are men and instruments of war? These are the things that mean naval construction. These are the things which the right hon. gentleman had in mind when he took the position which his friends behind him are taking and arguing, as my hon. friend from Mus-koka (Mr. Wright) did this afternoon in regard to the impossibility of doing anything in Canada. When my right hon. friend says that it will take twenty-five years for Canada to do what Australia has done in four, I say he is insulting Canadian manhood and Canadian intelligence. Why should he talk about Canada being master of her own destinies and deal in platitudes of that kind, and why should he appeal to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to come in like good boys and support this proposition? There is not a man on this side of the House w'ho does not regard this issue as a most fundamental one in the interests of the people of Canada.
The idea of this miserable makeshift proposal, a combination of disloyalty on the one hand and extreme professions of loyalty on the other hand, which is put forward simply for the moment in order to tide over a political condition-the idea of appeal-Mr. BORDEN.
ing to hon. gentlemen on this side of the House to give up their Canadian pride and fall in behind a policy of that kind! Why, the right hon. gentleman knew when he made that suggestion that there was no foundation for it, no hope even in his own mind that it would ever be accepted. This theory that Canada cannot do anything in the way of ship-building for twenty-five years is a nice proposition indeed to emanate from the party that has always gloried in having been the party that, in 1878, laid the foundation of the national policy. My hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Fripp) declared that he and his party were the true friends of Canadian labour and Canadian industry.
Hear, hear.

If my hon. friends
opposite have not wakened up to the fact that the very essence of this proposition is the denial of the fundamental basis of the national policy, they do not know what they are talking about. The Conservative party said to the people of Canada: ' Even though it be so much the worse for British connection, Canada proposes to establish a tariff which shall descriminate, if necessary, against the manufacturers of England in order that we may build up a manufacturing industry in Canada. That is what Sir John Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper said in this Parliament in 1877 and 1878, and that is what every man on the otheT side of the House has gloried in. Yet, to-day, they tell the people of this country that they have sunk so low that after nearly fifty years of Confederation, their position is so mean that they cannot hope for twenty-five years to come to engdge in an industry which men in other parts of the Empire have learned to engage in successfully in two or three years. Well might my hon. friend from Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), coming from a portion of this country where, even within a short period of time the steel industry of Canada has been built up so that to-day we have an industry there that exceeds in possibilities anything to be found in any other part of the British Empire, and equals in the character of its products anything even in the Motherland, a portion of the country where to-day they are in a position to roll plates, where within six months from now they will be able to give to the ship-building industry plates that might be used for the construction of vessels in the shipyards to carry on transportation or provide for the protection of commerce-I say well might that hon. gentleman say that the action of the Government was to throw to the dogs and the wolves the steel industry of the country, and the

labouring men engaged in it. To-day, this Government, after six months of tribulation in dealing with this measure, have discarded the theory that this is a gift to the weary Titan across the sea. This is no gift of money or grant of ships-it is nothing 'but a loan of ships. My right hon. friend began to minimize this on the 7th of April. This was only a loan of ships which he assured the House and the country and were to be returned whenever Canada provided for the oonstructiin of a naval system of her own. At that time I asked my right hon. friend to say whether his true permanent policy was not the policy which we advocate, the only permanent policy this country can ever have, and the right hon. gentleman knows it. It is the policy of speedy organization of a Canadian naval service which he stood for in 1909, which he spoke for in England, in his own constituency and all over Canada. I asked my hon. friend three days ago to tell this House frankly, before he submitted this measure to its final passage whether or not that was not his permanent policy. I ask him now, before we leave this committee, to be frank for once on this question, and tell us where he stands upon it. So far, we have had the most delightful evasions, we have had special interpretations put upon this proposition, one in one part of Canada to suit the electorate theTe and another in another part of Canada to suit an electorate differently minded. We have seen the delightful way in which the newspapers in your own constituency, Mr. Chairman (Mr. Blondin), have gilded this pill for consumption in that part of Canada, where men were wont, two years ago, to go up and down the land telling the people that Canada owed nothing to England, and that she ought not to have anything to do with naval contribution, or naval service. And we find in the I/Evenement newspaper in Quebec this statement of that wonderful policy forsooth we are asked to accept:
It is sufficient to read this Naval iBill to grasp the fact that there is no real question of sending a single cent to England, hut only a mere appropriation of a fixed sum which the Government spend in any way it pleases, and w'hich it need never spend at all if circumstances change some of these days; for the Bill specifies .no date, place, or conditions, or even any obligation to spend the money.
. . . The conclusion is, therefore, that the Naval Bill is simply a manifestation of friendship and of gratitude toward England -merely a moral object.
A nice title for this measure to bear 'a moral object'. There are various other kinds of 'objects' I might speak of as descriptive of it, but, we will be content with the beautiful language of the Postmaster General (Mr. Pelletier) in his newspaper wherein he, one of its own fathers, calls it a 'moral object.'

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The time allowed to
the hon. member has expired-unless the committee cares to-

I have until two
o'clock; I did not start until twenty minutes to two. So, this is not a gift of men, or money, or ships, to the Mother Country. And all these wild patriotic appeals in which hon. gentlemen have been indulging here and elsewhere have gone for naught-for nothing but 'a moral object' in which this Government, perhaps, may never spend a single dollar. The statement in this paper is a strong argument in support of the position taken by the hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) which we have been contending for for twenty-four hours, the position that, as this Bill is drawn, you are simply giving a blank cheque to this Government to do with as they please. My right hon. friend the leader of the Government, even in his last address on this question, apologetically says:	Gentlemen of Parliament, be
good enough to support this measure, because, even if we give the order to construct these ships, they will not be constructed before 1916 and by that time you will have had a chance to go to the country. But he said that nothing had been done about a permanent policy. Is he going to stand upon this as his permanent policy? Is this all he has?
Another contribution.
' Another contribution,' my hon. friend from Beauce says. But the leader of the Government has closed the door against that, because he has declared that he does not stand for contribution.
He has declared for both.

My right hon. friend has made such an ingenious speech that it is possible for him to declare for a contribution policy or for a construction policy, whichever suits him. I say again the right hon. gentleman ought to be more frank with the committee than he has been on this important matter. Before he forever shuts off discussion in committee on this important measure, he should tell the House and the people of this country where he really stands in the matter. There is not an hon. gentleman sitting behind the right hon. gentleman in this House who knows whether the leader of the Government to-day stands for a policy of contribution or a policy of construction. My right hon. friend is putting the gag upon Parliament; he is applying the closure and preventing free speech in order to prevent Parliament and the country from ascertaining from him

where he really stands in this matter. My right hon. friend, by virtue of his majority, and by introducing rules in a manner unconstitutional and never before heard of, may bring this discussion to a close, but let me ask my right hon. friend before he does	so if he	can	tell	the peoplewhether	this is a	gift	or	a loan ora moral	object lesson?	The	people willwant to know from the Conservative party and from its leader if they are in favour of the speedy organization of a Canadian naval service, just as Australia is, as New Zealand	is, and as	all	the	other great
nations of the Empire are; or whether they are in favour of a policy of contribution, a policy of humiliation for the Canadian people? And let me say that the people of Canada will in the end decide this question, and when that time comes they will support a policy under which Canadian pride, Canadian confidence and Canadian assertion of rights will find full and complete fruition.
Saturday, May 10, two a.m.

Mr. MEIGHEN; If you will excuse me, that is not the point. The point is this: the Prime Minister, as I understood it, rose and moved that we report this Bill.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is a matter of little importance who rose first. The question is whether or not my hon. friend (Mr. Carroll), who was told this afternoon that he could not move an amendment when he proposed to move it, can move it now. It is an important point whether under these rules we can move an amendment now or whether we are shut off from further discussion. I propose to discuss that point. I submit that the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) is perfectly in order in moving an amendment to this Bill before it can be taken out of committee. When he rose this afternoon to move his amendment, he was told that he could not move it. I thought the point was well taken, because the Prime Minister had moved the motion of which he had given notice yesterday evening and that motion had been adopted by the committee. He had moved:
That the further consideration of the second, third, fourth and fifth sections and of the proposed sixth section of this Bill, shall be the first business of the committee, and shall not further be postponed.
As that motion was agreed to, my hon. friend from South Cape Breton could not move an amendment until the committee had ordered that the first consideration of the second, third, fourth, fifth and sixth sections had been disposed of. Let us examine these rules. The motion was moved by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister acording to the rules. The rule saya that, if the House be in Committee, it can be moved:
That the further consideration of any resolution or resolutions, clause or clauses, section or sections, preamble or preambles, title or titles, shall be the first business of
the committee.
Mark the words. Shall not be the ' only ' business, but shall be the 'first' business

Other hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

I repeat, Sir, that you
did so. It looks as if we we were living in
Russia. We not only have the gag applied to us but we have had a private member of this House directing the Chairman as to what he should do. We have had enough of this farce during the last two or three months.
Sit down.

I will talk here as long as I want to. We have had men put in this Chair who had no right to be there and we have had the hon. member for Portage la Prairie coming down and telling them what they ought to do and what they ought not to do.

Sit down.
Other hon. MEMBERS: Go on.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member is
out of order.

I am making a few pertinent remarks, Mr. Chairman, something that should be said to you and I am the man who has got the sand to say it to you. I want the right hon. Prime Minister to take notice of what I have said. Now, I want to address myself to this amendment. It is necessary to use harsh language sometimes when we have exhibitions such as we have had to-night. I do not care whether the point of order taken by my hon. friend from Welland (Mr. German) is well taken or not. The father of these rules, the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, has admitted to the leader of the Opposition that he is right in his interpretation of them. The

Prime Minister has acquiesced in that construction. The whole question now is, can the Prime Minister of Canada by a ruse with his Chairman refuse to allow a member to wave an amendment?
Order. Sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I rule that the point of order is not well taken, and that no amendment can be made at this stage.
Shame.

I want to put a question to you, Mr. Chairman; under what rule is there a motion to be made that you report the Bill? I always heard you ask the Committee, ' Shall I report the Bill?' which means; has anybody else any other motion to make? You did not say that to-night, and if you had said it the member for South Cape Breton would have risen and made his motion, and you would have accepted it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The regular course is that somebody should make a motion that the committee rise; but ordinarily the Chairman assumes the motion has been made, and leaves the Chair without waiting for someone to make it.
With all due respect-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am now putting the motion that the Bill be reported.
Shame.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those in favour of the motion will please rise.
I move that you now leave the Chair.
Let me make my point of order, please.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The motion now before the committee is that I report the Bill. I ask those who are in favour of it to rise.
Some hon. MEMBERS; No, we won't rise.
Other hon. MEMBERS; Shame.
The CHAIRMAN; Those who are in favour of the motion will please say: ' aye.'
Some hon. MEMBERS; Aye.
Other hon. MEMBERS; No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those in favour of the motion will please rise.

Shame.
Some hon. members having arisen;

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Those against the motion will please rise.

Shame; don't
vote. Nobody vote on this side.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I declare the motion carried.
Mr. Speaker having resumed the Chair:
You have a false report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Blondin, Chairman of the Committee of the Whole-
No, no.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The report is not fair.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Blondin from the Committee of the Whole reports the Bill with an amendment.
Order. False report.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the Speaker is on his feet it is the duty of hon. members to preserve order. I have no doubt that hon. members are equally interested with me that the business of the House shall be conducted with decorum.
Where is the decorum on the other side?
The report is false.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The Nationalist gag.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I ask the hon. members of this House, as befitting what should be expected in Parliament, to join me in maintaining the dignity of Parliament and the prerogatives of this House in a proper and orderly way.

Why don't they respect the rules?
Mr. Oliver having risen in hie place:

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The prerogatives of this House have been usurped by the Government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
The Chairman made a false report to you, Sir.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When shall this report
be received?

No. Don't receive it.
Mr. BORDEN moved the adjournment of the House.	.
On the question being put:
We won't adjourn.
I desire respectfully to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that the Deputy Speaker has made a false report.
Order.
There was another motion before the Chair when he left the Chair; he ignored that motion, and the Speaker ought not to receive that report.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I want to say that it is not the right of a member to either criticize or reflect upon the conduct of the Chair in that way.
Oh.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. That can only be done by a substantive motion, and it can be done by giving notice at any time. That is the rule.	.

Mr. Speaker, you are
asking us to observe the rules, and we ask you to sustain the rights of the minority.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In my judgment, the best way to maintain the Tights of the minority is to maintain the rules.
Hear, hear.
The rules were broken by the Government.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rules are made for the minority as well as for the majority.
The rules were openly violated by the Chairman.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the House that the motion be carried?

No, no.
Other hon. MEMBERS: Carried.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I declare the motion
carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The House adjourned at 3.40 a.m., Saturday.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Monday, May 12, 1913.
